articles.title_orig: Webull stock suffers worst day in a year after lawmakers flag ties to China
articles.title_zh: Webull stock suffers worst day in a year after lawmakers flag ties to China
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Webull ( BULL ) stock plunged 19% on Wednesday after US lawmakers reportedly flagged that the company is "tied in structural ways" to China's government, risking its regulatory standing in the US.
The stock faced its worst daily drop since April 17, 2025, according to Dow Jones and FactSet market data. Over the past month, the stock has cratered by 40%.
On Wednesday, CNBC reported that a bipartisan House Select Committee on China assessment found that the company poses a national security risk and that concerns about its operations have "escalated" over the past year.
Webull is a digital investment platform headquartered in St. Petersburg, Fla. Yet the congressional report stated there was "a profound gap" between how the company marketed itself as a US company and how it is actually controlled.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the report said, per CNBC.
The company was founded in 2016 by former Alibaba ( BABA ) employee Anquan Wang and was affiliated with the Chinese holding company Hunan Fumi Information Technology. It went public on the Nasdaq via a special-purpose acquisition merger with SK Growth Opportunities in 2025.
Webull has 28.2 million users, and roughly 85% of its funded accounts are held by US users, according to SEC filings. The committee raised concerns that Webull's US customer data could be exposed should Webull be compelled to comply with Chinese laws and government requests.
Webull pushed back on the report, telling CNBC that it contained "significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions."

articles.title_orig: Lawmakers probe St. Pete stock trading firm’s Chinese ties
articles.title_zh: Lawmakers probe St. Pete stock trading firm’s Chinese ties
articles.content_orig:
Digital investment platform Webull , which counts 28 million global users , is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to U.S. finance, according to a bipartisan congressional panel's findings shared exclusively with CNBC.
The bipartisan House Select Committee on China in its new report being released Wednesday found "a profound gap" between Webull's public marketing as "an American company" and actual control of the St. Petersburg, Florida-based firm.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the committee found.
The panel asserted that national security concerns around the company have "escalated" since October 2025, when Webull began carrying customer cash directly, according to a regulatory filing the panel cited. The committee alleges that creates a "structural exposure of billions of dollars in American capital."
The committee said the company's corporate structure means the firm's "software development, data pipelines, and core engineering operations" are dependent on infrastructure subject directly to Beijing's laws. And those laws in China can compel firms to cooperate with the government in myriad ways, including data transfers.
Webull took issue with the report, saying via a spokesperson, "It is deeply disappointing that the Select Committee published a report containing significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions without ever seeking clarification from Webull." "Webull's U.S. business is conducted from its global headquarters in St. Petersburg, Florida and its office in New York City, while U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S.," the spokesperson said via email. "We remain prepared to address any questions directly and with the same transparency we bring to the SEC, FINRA, and regulators worldwide."
Webull's stock plummeted 18% in morning trading.
Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., told CNBC in a statement that Webull's "China-based operations put American investors and their data at risk."
"Using technology providers in mainland China and an opaque China-linked ownership structure, Webull exposes its data to our foremost adversary," said Moolenaar, who chairs the House committee that issued the report. "Investors should heed this information when choosing who they do business with."
Webull, which trades on the Nasdaq stock exchange, says it operates a "global network of licensed brokerages," offering investment services in 18 markets around the globe. The online brokerage says it provides retail and institutional investors with 24/7 access to global financial markets. Users of the platform can trade global stocks, exchange-traded funds, options, futures, fractional shares and digital assets on the service.
Former Alibaba and Xiaomi manager Wang Anquan founded Webull in 2016 . Its competitors include Robinhood , Charles Schwab and E-Trade .
The congressional committee, which had requested information from the company in 2024, said Webull represents a national security risk because "critical backend systems, personnel and data flows may remain exposed to the Chinese Communist Party's mandatory intelligence laws and coercive demands."
The committee said in its report that Webull Financial's "intricate corporate and technology framework" is tethered directly to China.
Webull Corp. is a Cayman Islands-incorporated holding company, and the report found it holds $24.6 billion in customer assets. And although the company has a U.S. holding company known as Webull Holdings (US) Inc., the report says the company's technology structure also includes Webull Technologies Pte. Ltd, which is a Singapore-based entity. And the report says Webull uses a mainland China-based subsidiary that supports technology development and platform operations. The company traces its origins to Hunan Fumi Information Technology Co., Ltd., a Chinese company that originally launched the business.
The release of the report comes on the heels of a largely friendly summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in September, and it comes ahead of further meetings between the two leaders later this year. It reflects concerns on Capitol Hill that the Chinese government could be planting seeds inside the U.S. financial system that could later be used to disrupt the American economy in the event of further conflict.
The committee also alleges Webull misrepresented the number of its China-based employees. In the report, the committee said the company initially told the committee it "does not have any offices or employees based in the PRC," and that "all Firm employees are located in the United States." But the committee says the firm remains operationally concentrated in China, with its mainland subsidiary, Hunan Weibu, growing to 863 employees, or 62% of the company's global workforce.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500, Nasdaq ease from record highs as Treasury yields climb
articles.title_zh: S&P 500, Nasdaq ease from record highs as Treasury yields climb
articles.content_orig:
The yields on key U.S. Treasury bonds touched fresh 24-year highs Wednesday, as the latest global bond sell-off picked up steam.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose as high as 5.36% and the 30-year Treasury yield hit 5.73% — the highest levels for each since 2002.
Benchmark government bonds in France and Italy also rose sharply. The yield on the U.K. 30-year government bond hit its highest level since 1998.
When bonds fall, their yields rise.
U.S. bond yields pulled back later in the day, following a Treasury Department auction of $39 billion worth of 10-year bonds, for which there was strong demand.
But at 5.3%, the yield on the auctioned bonds was the highest of any U.S. government sale of 10-year debt since November 2000.
“Bottom line, for whatever reason, likely the 24 yr highs in rates, brought out the buyers and resulted in a great auction,” wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners. “In response, the 10 yr yield has backed off to 5.27% from 5.31% just prior to the results.”
The bond rout had sent stocks tumbling early in the day, but as the decades-high yields eased, so did losses among the major stock indexes.
After notching record highs on Tuesday, both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq ended the day down about 0.2%. The Dow fell 341 points or 0.6%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small and medium sized companies, declined 1.3%.
European stock markets had seen steeper selling. The Stoxx 600 index ended lower by 1%, while benchmark indexes in France and Germany closed down by around 1.3%. Italy’s FTSE MIB index slid 2.5%.
As stocks fell, oil prices flipped between gains and losses, but largely hovered around their highly-elevated levels. Brent crude oil declined 0.5% but was still at more than $100 per barrel in afternoon trading.
The recent rise in bond yields only compounds the pain for governments around the world that have seen their borrowing costs soar since the start of the year.
Overnight, International Monetary Fund chief Kristalina Georgieva warned that governments urgently need to take steps to get their unprecedented debt under control.
She also predicted that government bond yields around the world would remain under pressure because of the ever-expanding artificial intelligence boom.
“Policymakers had a relatively easy ride over the last 17 years, as for all that time interest rates were stuck below GDP growth rates,” Georgieva said in a speech. “Higher interest rates now put an end to that.”
Her comments followed multiple reports that Elon Musk’s SpaceX is planning to raise $40 billion in cash to buy AI chips from Nvidia. NBC News has not independently confirmed the reports and SpaceX did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
But if the company follows through, that borrowed $40 billion would join hundreds of billions more in bond sales by AI-linked companies in recent years. The companies are using the money to build data centers and buy equipment with which to fill them.
Some economists believe that the vast sums of money being borrowed by private AI companies could pile additional pressure on government bond yields.
“France may be on the verge of a full-blown debt crisis,” wrote Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research on Sunday.
He noted that the yield on French 10-year government bonds has risen the most of any major economy this year. Coming in second  is the United States, while Italy, a country traditionally viewed as far more risky by the bond markets, comes in third.
Apollo economic strategist Huw van Steenis wrote in a Wednesday note, “Hyperscalers have raised $48 billion in bonds in European currencies this year, which is already more than triple the entire amount of 2025.”
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike severely unwell, ‘angry and confused’, says lawyer, after judge orders all execution evidence preserved – latest
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike severely unwell, ‘angry and confused’, says lawyer, after judge orders all execution evidence preserved – latest
articles.content_orig:
Tennessee Assistant Attorney General John W. Ayers, left, presents arguments during a court hearing, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn., as attorneys for Christa Pike request the Tennessee Department of Corrections to preserve all evidence related to her failed execution. George Walker IV/Pool AP hide caption
The Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville ordered Tennessee prison officials to preserve all evidence in connection with last week's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, including log books, medical waste and all messages sent or received by officials associated with the execution attempt.
"Anything in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," Judge I'Ashea Myles said.
The judge also granted a request from Pike's attorneys for "liberal access" to their client, ordering that prison officials will have two hours to respond to requests from lawyers for in-person visits with Pike.
Speaking outside the courtroom, Luke P. Ihnen, an assistant federal defender in Knoxville, told reporters that this was "just a first step of many to preserve and enforce Christa's constitutional rights after this unprecedented botched execution."
The hearing came a week after Pike was left hospitalized and in critical condition following the Sept. 30 execution attempt in which she was strapped to a gurney and administered two doses of pentobarbital, a barbiturate widely used in U.S. executions. But several minutes after the first dose, she said her arm was burning and asked whether it was supposed to feel that way. She then said, "Please try up on my shoulder higher."
Pike's attorneys said that after days of unconsciousness, Pike was awake again, speaking and continuing to receive critical medical care.
Randy Spivey, a post-conviction attorney representing Pike, called his client "a survivor."
"She survived sexual abuse [and] the rapes of multiple men. She survived a suicide attempt when she was 12 and she survived the state's attempt to execute her," he said. "She deserves answers about what was done to her and the people of Tennessee deserve those answers, too."
He said of the botched execution, "all of this was foreseen," because Pike has a medical condition that would make it difficult to insert an IV to deliver the lethal doses of pentobarbital.
Luke Ihnen, attorney for Christa Pike, speaks during a news conference after a judge ruled the Tennessee Department of Corrections must preserve all evidence related to the failed execution of Pike, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
Spivey, who was a witness to last week's failed execution, told NPR that after a second dose, Pike fell unconscious but continued breathing and making sounds like choking. It "went on for so long," he said.
Following the failed execution, Tennessee's top prison official, Frank Strada, resigned, and the state's governor, Bill Lee, halted executions through the end of the year and ordered an independent investigation into the state's capital punishment system.
It wasn't immediately clear whether that would affect a second attempt to execute Pike, but speaking at Wednesday's hearing, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General John Ayers said the decision on when or if to schedule a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.
Ihnen, one of the defense attorneys, said it would be "unconscionable that the state would try to execute her again."
FILE - This undated photo provided by the Tennessee Department of Correction shows Christa Pike. Tennessee Department of Correction/via AP hide caption
Pike was on death row for a murder she committed at age 18. In 1995, she and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow classmate in the Knoxville Job Corps. Shipp, who was a minor at the time of the crime, received life in prison without parole for his part in the murder.
In a clemency petition filed last month, Pike's attorneys asked that her sentence be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole, citing her history of childhood trauma.
"Local and national media covered Christa's trial in the midst of the 'Satanic Panic' of the 1990s," the attorneys said. "In truth, it was Christa's abusive boyfriend and co-defendant, Tadaryl Shipp, who was fascinated by satanic imagery."
The media at the time had "focused on the salacious parts of Christa's crime, disregarding the context of her youth, trauma, and mental illness," they added.
Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
Critics of the death penalty are outraged at what happened to Pike during the attempt to execute her.
"This failed attempt is the worst we've ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said in a statement .
The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization, said Pike was the first person in the history of capital punishment to survive after being injected with lethal drugs.

articles.title_orig: LACMA’s Alexander Calder Erewhon Smoothie Is What the Art World Deserves
articles.title_zh: LACMA’s Alexander Calder Erewhon Smoothie Is What the Art World Deserves
articles.content_orig:
Imagine you’re a hotshot young New York gallerist whose rapidly rising artist has been invited to show in a group exhibition at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA). But between this fall’s booths at Frieze London and Art Basel Paris, a detour to Venice, and micromanaging your unpaid interns, you can only go for a day. So, tragically, there’s no time to fit in your regular visit to Erewhon, for which there’s simply no New York equivalent, especially because the $36,000 initiation fee for the Kith Ivy padel club that houses the city’s only Erewhon tonic bar is prohibitive in this art market.
Well, I have good news for the few who can relate to these circumstances: LACMA announced this week that the Erewhon pop-up in its new David Geffen Galleries will now serve as the museum’s permanent cafe. Housed in a glass box beneath Peter Zumthor’s sprawling $720 million “ designed to disorient ” structure, the Erewhon cafe faces out toward Alexander Calder’s recently restored fountain, “ Three Quintains (Hello Girls) ” (1964).
Calder’s tripartite mobile is also the inspiration for a new (and pre-distressed) capsule apparel collection and a signature LACMA smoothie, made from organic mango, mandarin, pineapple, strawberry, and lion’s mane. The beverage's unnatural gray hue resembles the concrete of Zumthor’s design — only floating with blobs of Calderesque colors.
“This integration represents the perfect synergy between two brands inextricably rooted in Los Angeles culture,” Elizabeth Wiatt, senior vice president of strategic partnerships at LACMA, said in a press statement.
Much like the well-intentioned art world, whose ecosystem becomes more optimized but also more expensive and materialistic with each day, Erewhon is a far cry from the Taoist principles that guided its founders, Aveline and Michio Kushi, who established the first location in Boston in 1966. Today, the health-conscious “ premium ” grocery chain has become synonymous with a particular status-centric idea of LA, offering adaptogenic cocktails, celebrity-collaboration smoothies, and absurd oddities like a $12 cup of “ Sacred Water .”
For a museum that recently hosted the star-studded unveiling of Ed Ruscha's poster for Alejandro González Iñárritu’s new film Digger (2026), the Erewhon partnership is fitting. After all, it holds up a mirror to today's world, wherein overpaying for a smoothie somehow makes it more delectable, and institutional and commercial industry partnerships made under the guise of "community" are normalized.
Look no further than Erewhon President Josephine Antoci's euphemistic statement about the new LACMA cafe: “It’s a place for all to gather and make memories for years to come.”
The Ogunquit Museum of American Art and Bates College Museum of Art chronicle the life and work of under-recognized modern artist Carl Sprinchorn.
From activist art and trans aesthetics to lowriders, global skateboarding culture, and Vilém Flusser’s prescient vision of the screen age.
Experiment in the Sam Fox School’s expansive, state-of-the-art facilities, leveraging fellowship, residency, and research opportunities.
“Designed to Be Red: Native American & Indigenous Poster Works” is now on view at Poster House in New York City through February 21, 2027.

articles.title_orig: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.title_zh: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.content_orig:
The victim was working at the anti-plague institute in the Siberia city of Irkutsk
US President Donald Trump says he has a call set up with Vladimir Putin about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
Russian officials say they are investigating the death of the 28-year-old employee and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague. They insist there is no risk of an epidemic.
Trump told reporters on Wednesday evening he did not believe it was a bioweapon, adding "we're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so,"
"If you listen to them, it's under control," he said, referring to Russian authorities.
"We hope it is," he added. Reports emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation after the death.
Referring to China's initial response to the Covid pandemic, Trump said: "Well, China didn't say much, and Russia is not saying much either. But they do say they have it very much under control."
Pneumonic plague is a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
Trump said the US was in "deep discussions" with Russia, but the Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for more transparency from Russia, and requested further information on the lab tests on the individual who died.
"We don't yet have the full picture of this event," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said, adding that the WHO was also seeking "verification of media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause."
Ghebreyesus called on Russia to provide "timely, complete and transparent information" in order to clarify "conflicting reports" and help the WHO assess the potential public health risks.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice, and accused the media of reporting "false information".
The US has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.
Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after either breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
As the US and the WHO sought more information, the country's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, issued a statement saying "there are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region".
It said more than 90% of the people who had been in contact with the victim had "completed medical observation" and "no health disorders associated with infectious pathology were detected".
Neighbouring Mongolia's government has ordered "health surveillance" measures on its border with Russia, AFP news agency reported. The country's health ministry said it would "maintain continuous surveillance and monitoring to prevent potential risks".
This was a precautionary measure, it said, adding "the current risk level is low."
Lithuania's health ministry said it has made preparations to manage any possible case in the country.
Laboratory testing is available, patients would be isolated in infectious disease hospitals, contacts would be identified, and the country has the stocks of medicines suitable for treatment, according to Nerija Kaulakien, an adviser at the Ministry of Health's Communications Division, in an interview with ELTA news agency.
There was no evidence of "an increased risk of plague" at the moment, she said.
In the immediate wake of the laboratory worker's death, Russia's health watchdog had issued a statement saying the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology" and that testing found "no microorganisms related to her professional activities".
However, after this announcement, a pro-government federal news outlet deleted five posts mentioning a possible plague case, and authorities in the town of Baikalsk deleted a message advising against travel to Shelekhov because of a possible plague infection.
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:
contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
the inhalation of respiratory particles
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death .
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

articles.title_orig: Battle for the Darkspear Islands in World of Warcraft: Forever
articles.title_zh: Battle for the Darkspear Islands in World of Warcraft: Forever
articles.content_orig:
Off the coast of Dustwallow Marsh lies the Darkspear Islands, where a new battle is taking shape. In this 15v15 battleground, the Darkspear Raiders and Theramore Expeditionary Force clash for control of strategic footholds, a central flag, and the rewards waiting for those willing to fight for their faction.
Type of Map: 15v15 Capture Point with a Flag Capture Battleground Location: Off the Shores of Dustwallow Marsh Player Levels: 30-60 Victory Condition: First team to 2000 Points
Teams earn points by controlling four capture points across the Darkspear Islands. The more capture points your team controls, the quicker your team accrues points. A flag waits in the middle of the map, giving both teams another objective to fight over. Grab it, bring it to one of the bases your team has captured, and earn more points for your side. The first team to earn 2000 points wins!
You can queue for the battleground in a couple of ways. Visit a battlemaster located in any major capital city or in the Barrens (Kalimdor) seek out the Darkspear Raiders base (Horde) at the Merchant Coast or Theramore Expeditionary Force (Alliance) base located at Northwatch, where a portal will take you into the battle.
These bases also include vendors with reputation rewards you can acquire as you increase your standing with the Darkspear Raiders or Theramore Expeditionary Force. In these areas, you can also pick up quests for the battleground.
There is a reputation track for each faction for the Battleground: Darkspear Raiders and Theramore Expeditionary Force. They have gear and consumables that you can purchase including trinkets, rings, cloaks, weapons, armor pieces when hitting different reputation thresholds. And of course, there are quests for the Battleground. Turn in for Marks of Honor for reputation quests and unlock a short questline at Exalted to earn the faction's exclusive tabard.
Rally your allies, queue up for battle, and fight to secure the Darkspear Islands for your faction in WoW: Forever.j

articles.title_orig: Western civilisation is 'at an inflection point' Rubio says in speech overloooking Acropolis
articles.title_zh: Western civilisation is 'at an inflection point' Rubio says in speech overloooking Acropolis
articles.content_orig:
Standing before the Acropolis in Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio swept through the history of ancient Greece to the rise of American industry in a speech on Wednesday that portrayed western civilisation at risk of decline.
Rubio said the world was at an "inflection point". Nations, particularly in Europe, should return to ancient Greek values and "rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together".
"We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was here millennia ago," he said.
While he spoke of cooperation, Rubio also said "nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognise their common interests".
Rubio, often mentioned as a possible presidential candidate in 2028, touched on what he considered dangers in the world, such as "radical mullahs" in Iran and suicide bombers.
But most of his speech focused on a broader threat, describing the current period as a crossroads.
"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline," he said. "The next decade will write the story of the next century."
Rubio called for a return to the "classical understanding of politics and statecraft that the Trump administration hopes to reclaim - reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilisation".
That appeared to include renewed national pride, which he said the ancient Greeks had embraced, but the west had abandoned as "we felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world".
"The word 'nationalism' became a dirty word," he said. "So we tore down our monuments. We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.
"In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay."
Rubio's boss, President Donald Trump, has sought to carry out an "America first" agenda during both his terms in office, and taken a more confrontational stance toward traditional allies and in longstanding trade relationships.
Just six months ago, Trump again threatened to pull the US from the Nato alliance, which he has frequently criticised while pushing members to make larger contributions to defence.
Rubio's visit to the ruins of the Acropolis in Greece was part of his three-country tour of Nato allies that includes stops in Iceland and Portugal.

articles.title_orig: Supertanker chartered from Gulf Coast to China for $76 million, 10 times higher than pre-war level
articles.title_zh: Supertanker chartered from Gulf Coast to China for $76 million, 10 times higher than pre-war level
articles.content_orig:
(Subscribe to Brian Sullivan's "Power Insider" newsletter here .)
A supertanker was recently chartered to sail from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million, a source familiar told CNBC, as shipping costs soar globally due to the crisis in the Middle East.
The Alexandros was chartered by the trading firm Trafigura and is expected to load around Nov. 19, the source said. A normal rate for the route based on pre-war levels would be $7 million to $10 million.
The cost of the journey comes to $38 per barrel of oil assuming the tanker holds 2 million barrels. Shipping costs have exploded as the war in the Persian Gulf has led to a shortage of available tankers.
The Middle East producers are using a shuttle system to export oil through the Strait of Hormuz. A loaded tanker crosses the strait and then loads the oil onto another ship in the Gulf of Oman that takes the cargo to Asia. This system reduces the exposure to Iranian attack and has led to a rebound of crude exports through Hormuz. But it also requires a lot more ships to get the oil out of the Gulf.

articles.title_orig: Venture Global could ramp up LNG exports from Louisiana to China
articles.title_zh: Venture Global could ramp up LNG exports from Louisiana to China
articles.content_orig:
LNG supply chain disruptions caused by the Iran war are pushing China to look to the U.S., Bloomberg reports. Venture Global is discussing potential long-term contracts with at least three Chinese LNG importers, including PetroChina, to supply fuel from its export facilities in Louisiana, with PetroChina potentially purchasing more than 1 million metric tons of LNG annually. The discussions follow Venture Global’s rare recent agreement with a Chinese company for LNG deliveries beginning in 2030, signaling growing interest in U.S. gas despite trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.
China, the world’s largest LNG importer, is heavily reliant on Middle Eastern supplies, with nearly 30% of its LNG imports coming from Qatar last year. However, the Iran war has disrupted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and forced Qatar to shut a major export facility, raising concerns about the security of those supplies.
The near-closure of the strait since late February has driven up spot LNG prices in Asia and Europe, prompting China to scale back purchases.

articles.title_orig: Piep Haus Projects Opens in North Andover with Arthur Henderson’s Hand-Hewn World of Folk Story
articles.title_zh: Piep Haus Projects Opens in North Andover with Arthur Henderson’s Hand-Hewn World of Folk Story
articles.content_orig:
A pie safe, a sausage rope, and a model of the universe are among the curious objects in Peasant’s Burlesque, curated by Stace Brandt.
Quick Bit by Monica Lynn Manoski
Installation view, Arthur Henderson, “Peasant’s Burlesque,” Piep Haus Projects, 2026. Courtesy of Piep House Projects. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
Installation view, Arthur Henderson, “Peasant’s Burlesque,” Piep Haus Projects, 2026. Courtesy of Piep House Projects. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
It was a subtly crisp afternoon with soft light casting long shadows on the curving roads of North Andover as I drove with the windows down to my destination, Piep Haus Projects (PHP), a new experimental pop-up art space hosted at the home of artist Leah Piepgras. I followed a series of hand-painted arrows up the driveway to the far end of a previously shag-carpeted house with the unmistakable vibes of a swingers pad, now transformed into a living space, artist studio, and exhibition room. On my way in, a young person with flowing dark hair snaked past me, weaving in and out of sculptures, down through the yard to the edge of Lake Cochichewick and back through to where I stood.
PHP’s inaugural show features works by Arthur Henderson, a MassArt graduate who now lives and works in “relative isolation” (other than the company of his wife and son) in the woods of Western Connecticut. “Peasant’s Burlesque ,” curated by Stace Brandt, brings together seventeen larger works—all completed since the start of the year—including fourteen sculptures, two woodblock prints, and a Portrait of the Artist at Work in ink on paper, with twenty-two small-scale sculptures housed separately in a cabinet.
Arthur Henderson, Big Red (front), 2026. Plywood, Bondo, paint cabinetry, and plinth with variable objects inside. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
A six-foot-wide wooden chandelier with snuffed candles drew me into the exhibition room in the far end of the house. Titled Model of the Universe from the outside looking in , it’s suspended from the vaulted ceiling with a charcoal-colored chain. The work’s seven distinct arms invite your eyes to return again and again to trace the irregular edges, which, although cut from plywood, have a hand-drawn quality.
​ Big Red (2026), a chestnut-colored pie cabinet with doors splayed, holds a curious accumulation of hand-carved items including a pipe, medicine cup, and a stack of Porterhouse steaks. Its plywood back bears chiseled hands spelling P-I-E-S-A-F-E in American Sign Language. Underneath its four legs, an ebony trap door gives a sense of dark mystery. I found myself imagining who or what is beneath it.
​A glowing ember box serves as a pedestal for a hand-hewn baguette and beer can. Custom-crafted box crates elevate other lovingly shaped objects, including Milkcrib , a four-walled resting place for an imagined gallon of milk, and Decoy (Skull in Repose) , a small sculpture resembling a bruised and tilted three-dimensional heart. Throughout the room things are placed casually—like how you might find a space left if someone weren’t expecting company. On my way out, I passed a staircase guarded by a string of sausage links and a sign marked “Champagne Room,” which made me smile and want to stay and snoop around.
(left) Detail view of objects inside Big Red including Steaks , 2026. (right) Big Red (back), 2026. Plywood, Bondo, paint cabinetry, and plinth. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
The show exudes a whimsical, masculine energy, with each object serving as a breadcrumb to a larger narrative series the artist calls The Feast of the Butcher King . The objects in “Peasant’s Burlesque” are made from the perspective of the townsfolk who fall victim to the Butcher King in a retake on the folktale “Stone Soup.” The viewer enters a “set” where objects are contrived as offerings in exchange for the magic soup stone.
Brandt thoughtfully responded to the challenge of bringing Henderson’s purposely rough-hewn objects together with the newly renovated white cork-floored, multi-windowed project space. Henderson said, “What could’ve created a tension or competition instead feels very harmonious—a true conversation between the objects and their surroundings.”
​Arthur Henderson and Stace Brandt will be present with the work on Sunday, October 25, 2026, from 1:00 to 6:00 p.m. Between now and then, the space is open by appointment. Reach out to leah.piepgras@gmail.com for availability.

articles.title_orig: France suspends use of stun grenades to police student protests
articles.title_zh: France suspends use of stun grenades to police student protests
articles.content_orig:
French police will no longer use stun grenades on student protesters after a 15-year-old lost his hand at a demonstration over school conditions.
Reuters reported the government ordered law enforcement agencies to stop using the grenades to hold back protesters.
The northern French newspaper La Voix du Nord reported Monday that the student was holding one of the grenades launched during the protest when it went off, and he also lost part of his lower arm.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the incident, along with 17 other cases, has been referred to police for investigation. Schools across the country have been damaged, with 24 reporting damage expected to cost $22 million to $34 million to fix.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Saudi Arabia launches air safety probe into flydubai incident, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Saudi Arabia launches air safety probe into flydubai incident, sources say
articles.content_orig:
FlyDubai faces renewed scrutiny over its pilot screening after an Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked his captain with an ax on an Israel-bound flight, raising questions about whether the airline's rapid expansion outpaced its ability to vet recruits.
The Sept. 30 attack aboard Flight FZ1073 sent the Boeing 737 MAX into a steep descent with 182 people aboard. Passengers and crew subdued the attacker, and another pilot traveling on the aircraft landed it in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, has classified the incident as a terrorist attack. Investigators continue examining physical and digital evidence, the suspect's motives, and any related links. Authorities have not announced final investigative findings.
Hamam al-Hammami, 29, joined FlyDubai in February. Oman Air previously barred him from flying over concerns about extremist views and reassigned him to administrative work, The Associated Press reported, citing officials and people familiar with the matter.
Royal Air Maroc, Morocco's national carrier, confirmed that he completed three months of theoretical training in 2025 but was not selected for employment. The training was part of its application process, ABC News reported .
The Wall Street Journal reported that FlyDubai conducted a criminal background check before hiring him but did not contact Oman to vet his experience, citing a person familiar with the process.
In a separate report Wednesday , the Journal said that al-Hammami told investigators he sought airlines and routes that would take him to Israel and nearly carried out an attack during the summer before reconsidering, according to people briefed on the inquiry.
New Zealand police said Tuesday that he completed part of his flight training there between November 2018 and May 2019 for a British company. Australian counterterrorism authorities are also examining his ties to that country, Reuters reported .
Saudi authorities detained al-Hammami after the emergency landing and transferred him to the United Arab Emirates last Thursday. The airline and Emirati authorities have not publicly identified him, Reuters reported, while investigators in several countries continue reviewing his travel and training history.
FlyDubai says it is cooperating with investigators and coordinating with government authorities and regulators.
"The safety and wellbeing of our passengers, crew and operations remain our highest priority," the airline said in a statement .
Flights to and from Israel remain suspended while the investigation continues. The carrier says it will review the suspension as additional information becomes available and help passengers find alternative travel arrangements.
The scrutiny comes after years of growth. FlyDubai's workforce expanded from 3,682 employees at the end of 2021 to 6,763 at the end of 2025, according to company financial reports .
The airline carried a record 15.7 million passengers in 2025 and earned $531 million after tax. Its network reached 140 destinations in 58 countries, while its fleet grew to 97 aircraft.
The carrier serves destinations including Kabul and Damascus, providing links to places many Western airlines avoid.
"FlyDubai continued the whole time, they didn't stop, which is remarkable," said Yoel Guzansky, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies.

articles.title_orig: Martin Moran's Other Bodies Sets World Premiere Off-Broadway
articles.title_zh: Martin Moran's Other Bodies Sets World Premiere Off-Broadway
articles.content_orig:
This latest solo play is the third in Moran's trilogy, following The Tricky Part and All the Rage .
October 07, 2026 By Logan Culwell-Block
Other Bodies , a new solo play from Martin Moran , will make its world premiere Off-Broadway via Barrow Group, with performances beginning November 19 ahead of a November 23 opening night.
The work is the third in Moran's trilogy of solo works, following the 2004 Obie-winning The Tricky Part and 2013's Lucille Lortel Award-winning All the Rage . As with the earlier works, Seth Barrish is directing.
“For more than 20 years, these solo pieces have been a way for me to wrestle with questions I don’t know how to answer,” shares Moran in a statement. “ Other Bodies grew out of the pandemic, a moment when we were suddenly forced apart from one another, but it became an exploration of something much larger: how we live with difference, how we recognize experiences that aren’t our own, and how we find our way back to one another. I didn’t set out to write a trilogy, but returning to this form with Seth, and bringing this third piece to The Barrow Group, where The Tricky Part first began, feels like completing a circle.”
Moran's Broadway credits include roles in Spamalot , Cabaret , Titanic , Wicked , Big River , and Funny Girl , along with the Off-Broadway premiere of Floyd Collins .
Tickets are at BarrowGroup.org .

articles.title_orig: Iowa Attorney General sues video surveillance company over ties to China
articles.title_zh: Iowa Attorney General sues video surveillance company over ties to China
articles.content_orig:
DES MOINES, Iowa (KCRG) - Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird announced Wednesday that she is suing surveillance video company ADI Global Distribution Inc.
The suit says ADI hid that the cameras manufacturers, Hikvision and Dahua, have close ties to the Chinese military.
The suit says both camera makers are on a list of foreign entities that pose a national security risk to the United States.
It says ADI has deceived Iowans for years by selling the products as their own brand.
It also accuses Hikvision and Dahua of deliberately engineering “backdoor” security vulnerabilities into their cameras that can be exploited for eavesdropping or criminal activity.
In a statement, Bird said “These China-made cameras are making Iowans’ private information — everything from where each room is in your home, who lives there, your routine, and even passwords — available to the Chinese government and military.”
This is the second lawsuit by Bird this week against China-aligned companies .

articles.title_orig: Fed officials see another hike coming, but no sign as to when, minutes show
articles.title_zh: Fed officials see another hike coming, but no sign as to when, minutes show
articles.content_orig: Federal Reserve officials expect they will raise interest rates again before the end of the year to head off inflation that has run above target for more than five years, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday. But the meeting summary provided no indication of when specifically policymakers expected to raise benchmark rates – only that persistently higher prices and a stable labor market likely would lead to a second hike this year. The Fed next decides on rates on Oct. 28 and then again on Dec. 9. "With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end," the document stated. That position came with a note of caution. "Participants emphasized, however, that they approached each meeting with an open mind and decisions at future meetings would depend on incoming information and its implications for the outlook and the balance of risks," the minutes said. Coming off the meeting, which featured tough inflation talk from Chairman Kevin Warsh during his subsequent news conference, markets started betting the Fed would follow the Sept. 16 hike with another move at the late October meeting. However, recent inflation data and comments from leading Fed officials indicate that at least for October, another increase is unlikely. The Fed's preferred gauge – the personal consumption expenditures price index – showed core inflation at 3% for August and headline at 3.4%. While both readings were still well north of the central bank's 2% target, they were considerably lower than expectations, benefiting in part from changes in the way some of the inputs are calculated. Discussion at the September meeting showed officials see risks that inflation will prove sticky, while the labor market is "close to maximum employment" and economic growth overall has picked up. The vote to raise the benchmark funds rate by a quarter percentage point was unanimous, despite prior indications that several key officials were reluctant to hike. "Many participants emphasized that a higher path for the target range would be prudent on risk-management grounds, providing insurance against inflation remaining persistently above target due to stronger-than-expected demand or further adverse supply shocks," the summary said. As a group, the Federal Open Market Committee indicated one more hike this year, then none in 2027. Of the 18 FOMC officials who submitted forecasts, 16 said they expected another increase. Warsh has not submitted a forecast since taking the position in May. During his news conference, he described the rate rise as removing "a dose of accommodation" from monetary policy, a remark that Wall Street analysts pored over and took to mean that additional increases could be on the way. But several other officials since then have stressed that the Fed doesn't need to rush, while inflation data has been at least a bit more encouraging even if short-term expectations have risen considerably. Market-based indicators for inflation are still elevated, and a fresh survey released Wednesday by the New York Fed showed consumer fears over rising prices in the next year are at their highest since May 2023. Treasury yields have been soaring as well, hitting levels not seen since 2002. Officials at the meeting discussed the rise in yields, attributing them to expectations for higher rates from the Fed as well as the build-out in artificial intelligence and solid economic growth. Staff economists also noted that some of the surge may have come from "uncertainty related to the U.S. Treasury's announcement and implementation of the buyback program." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in August announced his department would ramp up its buybacks of already-issued long-dated debt. However, the move has had little impact on yields, which are around their highest levels since 2002.

TOWSON, Md. , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DEWALT, a Stanley Black & Decker brand renowned for relentless innovation on the jobsite, today announced that the world's first fleet-capable, downward drilling robot, DALE™, has been named a winner in Fast Company's 2026 Next Big Things in Tech Awards. The awards recognize innovative technologies developed by established companies, startups, and research teams that are making meaningful progress toward transforming the lives of consumers, businesses, and society. This year's innovations demonstrate the potential to create significant impact in the years ahead.
As the only tool manufacturer represented in the program, DALE was recognized in the "Enduring Impact: 15+ Years in Business" category honoring companies with an established track record of navigating history, culture, and evolving product lines to continue driving tomorrow's progress.
After earning strong industry attention at World of Concrete earlier this year, the robot has entered the market as a breakthrough solution optimized for data center construction. As data center development accelerates at an unprecedented pace, rapid execution has become a key advantage for hyperscalers working to bring new computing capacity online. Designed to dramatically improve how concrete drilling is performed, DALE brings a new level of speed, safety, and operational efficiency to the jobsite. Its arrival marks a major step forward for the industry, raising the bar for innovation at a time when faster, smarter building methods are more critical than ever.
"It is incredibly meaningful to see this work acknowledged by Fast Company ," said Bill Beck, President, Tools & Outdoor, Stanley Black & Decker. "Our teams set out to address a major challenge facing large scale infrastructure projects: how to help crews move faster without compromising consistency, safety, or control. This recognition reflects the strength of that effort and the value of bringing advanced automation to one of the most demanding construction environments. Working alongside August Robotics, we have introduced innovation that helps customers increase output, simplify execution, and better support the pace of modern building."
During the pilot program, the downward drilling robot achieved drilling speeds up to 10 times faster than conventional methods, helped reduce schedules by more than 300 weeks across 44 phases of data center construction, and delivered over 99% accuracy across more than 385,000 holes. With fast-swap batteries and remote monitoring, DALE™ is built to maximize uptime and support continuous drilling operations. Features such as automatic dust extraction and AI-driven quality assurance help leave sites clean and ready for immediate MEP installation, accelerating downstream work. Built on August Robotics' advanced autonomous, fleet-ready platform, DALE™ provides efficient, high-volume drilling for server rack stops and MEP supports, while strengthening DEWALT's broader data center offering alongside its PERFORM AND PROTECT™ tools and ICC anchoring solutions.

articles.title_orig: World leaders solemnly mark 3 years since Oct. 7, as Hamas and Iran celebrate anniversary
articles.title_zh: World leaders solemnly mark 3 years since Oct. 7, as Hamas and Iran celebrate anniversary
articles.content_orig:
The Nova music festival memorial site on Oct. 07, 2026.
The world changed when Hamas attacked Israelis on Oct. 7, 2023 , catalyzing devastating conflict throughout the region . But within Israel, political sentiments have changed surprisingly little.
To some, the attack fulfilled long-term right-wing warnings that Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza would yield disaster; and the attack was incontrovertible proof that Palestinians will never live in peace with Israel.
Israeli left-wingers, for their part, have long held that a festering military rule over Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, and failure to reach peace, would inevitably lead to violent conflagration. For them, Oct. 7 only proved that they had been right all along.
The standoff raises crucial questions. In three years since Oct. 7, how has the attack changed Israeli society? And how will the answer affect upcoming elections in Israel?
To be sure, there have been cataclysmic changes in Israel, and the Middle East at large, since Oct. 7. The war in Gaza that began that day has become Israel’s longest war. A relatively stable ceasefire with Lebanon from 2006 to 2023 ended when Hezbollah, a Shi’a militia group, fired on Israel the day after Hamas’ attack; after multiple escalations since then, the current ceasefire is precarious. Israel and the U.S. have waged two full-blown wars with Iran, and the Middle East is still threatened by spin-off conflicts.
The losses Israelis suffered on Oct. 7 and since then have affected the country collectively and profoundly. For two years, many Israelis went from demonstration to demonstration demanding that their government prioritize a deal with Hamas to release Israeli hostages. Hundreds of thousands have spent the last three years in and out of active reserve duty.
Since 2023, Israel has seen record levels of emigration and growing international isolation. Sixty-one percent of Israelis told pollsters for the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) that the national mood is poor .
Moreover, the destruction of Palestinian life and society , still ongoing , will one day force a terrible reckoning within Israel.
What’s less visible, and more surprising, is what has stayed the same. Israelis’ attitudes towards Palestinians, occupation, and conflict have become more extreme. But I would argue that Israeli public opinion today says much more about how Israel had changed prior to Oct. 7. The change in national attitudes since that fateful day has been moderate and consistent with what came before.
In December 2022, almost a year before Oct. 7, support for peace through a two-state solution hit a historic low. In the joint Palestinian-Israeli survey I conduct together with colleagues at Tel Aviv University and the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, support stood at 39% of Israelis that year—the lowest since the 1990s. Among Jewish respondents, just 34% supported a two-state solution, and 37% believed Israel should permanently annex the West Bank while Palestinians would have limited rights.
When we conducted the study again in mid-2024, Jews were twice as likely to support a single, Israeli-dominated unequal state as they were to support two states.
Palestinian attitudes in 2022 were similar. Just one-third supported two states. Both sides showed a mirror-image majority who distrusted the other. In surveys by the IDI from that same time, 59% of Jewish Israelis defined themselves as right-wing; just 12% said they were left-wing.
What changed after Oct. 7? This July, the Tel Aviv University Peace Index survey found that support for two states stood at 31%, an eight-point decline in the four years since 2022. Now, IDI surveys find that just over 60% of Israeli Jews describe themselves as right-wing, just a few points higher than late 2022.
Israel has changed, but this change began years before Oct. 7 2023. In 2010 , no fewer than 71% of Israelis supported a two-state solution in the joint surveys. The years that followed were plagued by stagnation and dissipation of any peace process, regular wars with Hamas, and a heavily nationalist government in Israel. It stands to reason that these phenomena pushed Israeli society further to the right. Support for the two-state solution eroded slowly, then rapidly by the end of the decade.
That shift was self-reinforcing: the more right-wing Israelis became (primarily the Jewish population), the more elected leaders took ever-more radical positions such as supporting settlement expansion and de facto annexation in the West Bank. In 2019, Prime Minister Netanyahu began referring to extending sovereignty over parts of the West Bank, or de jure annexation . The current government accelerated those processes drastically.
Study after study shows that Arab citizens of Israel have remained the strongest supporters of peace, before and after the current wars. But with Jewish Israeli and Palestinian attitudes so dismal in the years before Oct. 7, the chances of resurgent violence almost seemed inevitable.
In other words, most Israelis did not radically transform their worldview after Oct. 7. In fact, hardline political trends were among the many factors contributing to the terrible escalation to begin with.
Another thing that hasn’t changed in Israel during the last three years of war: hopes for peace. The number of Israeli Jews who self-describe as left-wing has barely shifted. In a May survey for the Institute for National Security Studies, about 20% of the total population, Jews and Arabs, define themselves as left-wing, and a similar share typically say they are centrist. These groups embrace a commitment to democracy, liberal values, separation of religion and state, and reject the religious fundamentalism of the current government.
The left remains committed to peace via diplomacy and Palestinian self-determination. In a mid-2025 survey I conducted for a peace organization called A Land for All, where I am also an active member, the large majority of self-defined left-wing Israelis, and nearly half of centrists, supported a basic two-state solution.
Do peace attitudes even matter, when there is no peace process? That may be theoretical for now, but elections aren’t. Israelis will be voting on Oct. 27. Polls show the voters deeply divided , just as they were in the elections held between 2019 and 2022.
Netanyahu’s far-right coalition is not doing well. Nearly all polls show his coalition parties well below their actual result in 2022. And most mainstream polls show a consistent majority for today’s opposition parties.
At first glance, these shifts might seem antithetical. Aren’t these ideological and electoral trends moving in contradictory directions: more right-wing, but a majority against the current government?
It turns out that even the Israeli electoral contradiction is not new. During the five elections from 2019 through 2022, a majority of Israelis were right-wing and voted for right-wing parties. But to form a coalition, some of those parties no longer supported Netanyahu and refused to join a coalition under his leadership. Netanyahu therefore commanded only about half the seats in parliament following four of these cycles. Neither side had a clear or firm coalition majority, and the country was thrown into electoral turmoil five times over.
But if all mainstream polls show the anti-Netanyahu parties winning, including right-wing opposition parties, shouldn’t that mean a decisive outcome against him this time? Not quite: no poll shows Israel’s Jewish, Zionist parties reaching a majority in October.
And in Israel’s right-wing, populist discourse, the main opposition party leaders opposed to Netanyahu now, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman, with similar statements from frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot , insist that parties representing Arab citizens must not be part of a coalition after Oct. 7. Microsoft has finally given us the all-important pricing and availability details for its flagship Surface Laptop Ultra device, which it first unveiled back in June . During its October 7th keynote in San Francisco, Microsoft confirmed that Surface Laptop Ultra would begin shipping on October 16 , with pre-orders going live today starting at $2,599.
That entry-level price is on the more expensive side, but it's not as bad as many were expecting it to be. That entry-level price nets you the Surface Laptop Ultra with a 15-inch mini-LED screen, a large haptic trackpad, three USB-C ports (one of which is very unique), and the 18-core RTX Spark with 5120 GPU cores and 24GB RAM.
While the entry-level model isn't for high-end local AI development and agent work, it should be more than capable for video editing, photo creation, data crunching, light gaming , and 3D modeling work.
Alongside pricing and availability, Microsoft also revealed that the Surface Laptop Ultra is the world's first laptop to feature a breakaway USB-C port , similar to Apple's MagSafe and its own Surface Connect. Breakaway cable design means if you ever trip over the cable while the laptop is plugged in, it won't yank the entire laptop off your desk.
Breakaway ports have only ever really been possible on proprietary ports, as they use magnets to ensure the cable remains attached when in use. It's never been attempted on a universal standard before, which is what makes the Surface Laptop Ultra's breakaway port so special. It's a standard USB-C port, capable of taking any USB-C peripheral you can throw at it.
Surface Laptop Ultra is Microsoft's most expensive and most powerful Surface PC ever made. The high-end configs are designed for intensive AI developer workloads such as running large 120B parameter models locally, enabling complex agentic AI workloads and experiences.

articles.title_orig: Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is available for preorder for $5,999
articles.title_zh: Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is available for preorder for $5,999
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft’s high-end AI mini PC for developers starts shipping in November.﻿
Microsoft’s high-end AI mini PC for developers starts shipping in November.﻿
Microsoft’s Nvidia-powered Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is available for preorder now and is slated to ship in November for just about $6,000. It’s pricier than the DGX Spark mini PC Nvidia launched last year, but PC prices have been climbing due to shortages of RAM and other components .
The Dev Box’s flat, 3D-printed anodized aluminum chassis doubles as a heatsink and resembles the top vents on an Xbox Series X. It was introduced alongside the new Surface Laptop Ultra and runs on Nvidia’s Arm-based RTX Spark platform and 128GB of unified memory. With that much memory, along with a 100-watt thermal envelope and Nvidia’s Tensor cores, you could probably get an impressive gaming experience on the Dev Box. But as its name suggests, it’s mainly aimed at developers. It’s optimized for running local AI, including “models exceeding 120B parameters,” for tasks like testing AI models, prototyping AI agents, or running AI coding tools on-device.
The Dev Box is also one of Microsoft’s Project Zenith devices , so it ships with a developer-optimized Windows 11 Pro setup and some preinstalled developer tools, including Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub CLI, GitHub Copilot, WSL, Python, and Node.

articles.title_orig: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.title_zh: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.content_orig:
Tulane Law School’s longstanding strength in comparative law was on full display in Berlin, where four faculty members took on prominent scholarly roles at one of the world’s most important gatherings of comparative law experts.
Tulane professors Vernon Valentine Palmer, James Gordley, Ronald J. Scalise Jr. and Mateusz Grochowski served as reporters at the 22nd General Congress of the International Academy of Comparative Law, held Sept. 28-Oct. 2 at Humboldt University of Berlin. Tulane faculty had the largest delegation and produced more reports for the gathering than faculty from any other U.S. law school.
Their roles included some of the congress’ most significant scholarly assignments. Palmer served as a general reporter, bringing together reports from 19 countries, while Gordley served as a special reporter. Scalise and Grochowski each represented the United States as national reporters on separate topics.
The strong showing is indicative of Tulane Law’s unique place in comparative and civil law scholarship, a tradition rooted in Louisiana’s mixed legal system and sustained by generations of internationally recognized scholars.
The International Academy of Comparative Law, founded in 1924, brings together leading scholars from legal systems around the world. Its General Congress is held every four years and has been described as the “World Congress of Law,” drawing roughly 1,000 scholars from more than 70 countries to Berlin this year.
Palmer, the Thomas Pickles Professor of Law and a globally recognized authority on mixed legal systems, served as general reporter for “Mixed Jurisdictions and Mixed Legal Systems from Around the World.” In that leadership role, Palmer synthesized 19 individual country reports examining the distinctive mix of legal traditions within each system.
Gordley, the W.R. Irby Distinguished University Research Professor, served as a special reporter for a panel examining “Contractual Fairness in the Rebirth of an Idea.” His report explored the distinction between an unfair contract and a “bad bargain,” and how legal systems around the world determine where one ends and the other begins.
Scalise, the Eason-Weinmann Chair in International and Comparative Law, served as a U.S. national reporter on “Trusts in Non-Common Law Systems,” examining the subject through both U.S. and Louisiana perspectives.
Grochowski also represented the United States as a national reporter, addressing “Innovative Complements and Substitutes for Contracts” and examining emerging alternatives to traditional contractual relationships in American law.
The reports by Tulane faculty, along with those of other U.S. scholars participating in the congress, are published in the American Journal of Comparative Law , one of the leading journals in the field.
Tulane’s influence extended beyond the congress’ scholarly program.
The Berlin gathering coincided with the annual meeting of the American Society of Comparative Law, the leading U.S. organization devoted to the comparative study of legal systems and traditions. Two Tulane professors hold leadership positions in the organization: Scalise serves as treasurer and Sally Brown Richardson, the A.D. Freeman Professor of Civil Law, serves as parliamentarian. Both helped lead the society’s business meeting in Berlin.
Tulane’s leadership in the field will come home to New Orleans next year.
In fall 2027, Tulane Law will host the American Society of Comparative Law’s annual conference, bringing more than 100 comparative law scholars from around the world to the law school for a three-day examination of “The Role of Comparative Law in a Global (and Sometimes Anti-Global) World.”
The gathering will put Tulane at the center of an international scholarly conversation that has long been part of the law school’s identity, and one in which its faculty continue to play leading roles.

articles.title_orig: FBI says it thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teen it supplied with an assault rifle
articles.title_zh: FBI says it thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teen it supplied with an assault rifle
articles.content_orig:
The 18-year-old had been under investigation for nearly two years.
MINNEAPOLIS -- The FBI thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teenager after agents supplied him with an assault rifle, authorities announced Wednesday.
The 18-year-old had been under investigation for nearly two years, trading messages with a confidential informant, before agents sold him the rifle and ammunition, according to a federal complaint described by U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen.
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, was arrested Tuesday in a public park after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of ISIS for an AK-47 and 200 rounds of ammunition, according to the criminal complaint.
In text messages with a confidential FBI source, Mohamud repeatedly affirmed his intent to carry out an attack to kill non-Muslims, the complaint said. It was not immediately known if the teen had an attorney who might speak on his behalf.

articles.title_orig: Germany’s Merz vows to fight ‘extremism’ after AfD, far-left election gains
articles.title_zh: Germany’s Merz vows to fight ‘extremism’ after AfD, far-left election gains
articles.content_orig:
Chancellor ⁠Friedrich Merz has hit out at what he called political “extremism” in Germany after recent stinging defeats in local elections to far-right and far-left parties.
“This is a task for ⁠our society as ⁠a whole, and it is ⁠one I intend ⁠to play ⁠my part in,” he said on Wednesday at an ‌event in Berlin.
Merz said “extremism” was forcefully making its way into the country’s parliaments, a day after a member of the far-right Alternative for ‌Germany (AfD) was elected president of the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt and the Left Party won out in Berlin’s state election last month.
“Anyone who casts their vote for ⁠the AfD is ⁠playing the extremists’ game and undermining credibility,” ⁠Merz said. “In ⁠any case, this is incompatible with the values of ‌my party, the CDU [Christian Democratic Union of Germany].”
Despite winning the vote in the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD fell three seats short of the absolute majority it had had sought. AfD lawmaker Tobias Rausch won the presidency of the parliament in the eastern German state Tuesday, backed by the left-populists in a secret ballot.
Founded in 2013 as a Eurosceptic movement, the AfD won over voters with an increasingly hardline opposition to immigration after about a million people fled to Germany in 2015, many of them from war-torn Syria.
The party has since become a dominant political force in much of eastern Germany, especially among voters disillusioned with mainstream parties, though most traditional parties have pledged not to enter coalitions with the AfD.
Merz’s comments followed the far-left Left Party’s victory in the Berlin state election on September 20, in another defeat for the chancellor’s ruling Christian Democrats.
Lead ‌candidate Elif Eralp campaigned on the soaring cost of housing in the German capital and immediately promised to follow through with a pledge to nationalise private housing associations that account for a large share of the city’s housing stock.
The result, which roughly doubled the party’s previous score, could see her become the first mayor of Berlin from the Left Party, which grew out of the former East German communist party following the reunification of the country 36 years ago.
Eralp, the 45-year-old daughter of left-wing Turkish parents who fled a coup in 1980, said the increasingly difficult rental situation was the biggest social problem in the capital.
She promised to proceed with nationalising the housing associations she said drove property speculation, in accordance with a referendum from 2021 in which 58 percent of voters backed a proposal to promulgate the move.
While the AfD has attracted most attention, the ⁠Left Party has also benefitted from a general turn against the mainstream centre-left and centre-right parties.
Meanwhile, Merz has received a record low approval rating . Earlier this month, a survey by Germany’s public broadcaster ARD found that only one in 10 respondents were satisfied or very satisfied with his performance, the lowest figure for any chancellor since the survey began in 1997.
Another major election test will come in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany’s most populous state, where voters are set to elect a new parliament in April.

articles.title_orig: Minnesota man accused of plotting Mall of America attack, pledging allegiance to ISIS: FBI
articles.title_zh: Minnesota man accused of plotting Mall of America attack, pledging allegiance to ISIS: FBI
articles.content_orig:
The FBI announced the arrest of an 18-year-old Minnesota man who allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America.
An 18-year-old Minnesota man who allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America was arrested after buying an AK-47-style rifle, magazines and ammunition from an undercover FBI employee, according to newly filed federal court documents.
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud had allegedly spent months discussing his desire to carry out an attack, telling an FBI confidential source in September, "I can’t wait until I kill kuffar man. October 24 is the day insha Allah," according to an affidavit filed in federal court in Minnesota .
When the source later asked why he had chosen Oct. 24, Mohamud allegedly pointed to a "Hmong Arts Celebration" at the Mall of America, saying it would have "a lot of people," the affidavit states.
WOMAN’S ALLEGED ISIS RADICALIZATION UNFOLDED ONLINE BEFORE CAPITOL BOMB PLOT: COURT DOCS
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, was arrested after FBI officials say he allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America. (U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota)
"Muhammad met with someone he believed to be a loyal member of ISIS to attempt to purchase an AK-47 rifle, knowing it would be used in a felony or federal crime of terrorism," Special Agent in Charge, FBI Minneapolis Field Office, Christopher Dotson said at a press conference Wednesday. "Mohammed planned to use the gun he bought in a high-traffic public area just a few weeks' time in support of a designated foreign terrorist organization."
Mohamud is now charged with knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition while knowing or having reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony and federal crime of terrorism.
The Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota. (Michael Siluk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images, File)
FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital in a statement that the suspect "allegedly obtained a weapon he hoped to use in a mass casualty attack in support of ISIS, but this FBI arrested him and put a stop to his plans."
"Once again, this FBI is moving more effectively than we ever have before at stopping terrorists before they can attack Americans – with over 1,100 individuals prevented from conducting attacks, over 4,000 foreign terrorist organization related disruptions and arrests, a 38% increase, and more," Patel said. "We will continue to use every resource we have to detect and prevent acts of terrorism and wipe out their networks all over the country. Thank you to FBI Minneapolis, who did an outstanding job in the investigation and likely saved lives."
FBI Director Kash Patel conducts a news conference at the Department of Justice. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)
President Donald Trump also praised the FBI’s handling of the case while speaking to reporters Wednesday.
"I did hear about it. And they did a great job. The FBI did a great job," Trump said. The arrest capped an FBI investigation that began around December 2024 and eventually involved a confidential human source who communicated extensively with Mohamud over encrypted messaging and social media platforms, according to investigators.
Those conversations initially centered on Mohamud allegedly wanting to leave the United States and join al-Shabaab, the Somalia-based terrorist organization. In May, he allegedly told the source he was "so excited to make hijrah" and wanted to go to Somalia, get married and "fight the enemies of Allah." He said he planned to work for about six weeks to save $2,000 for a plane ticket, according to the affidavit.
By July, however, investigators say his plans had changed.
Mohamud allegedly told the source he did not have enough money to travel to Somalia and wrote, "so i will do attack here." He later discussed buying two pistols online and going to the Mall of America or the Minnesota State Fair around Christmas, according to the affidavit.
DENVER MAN'S ESCAPE EXPOSES CHILLING TREN DE ARAGUA KIDNAPPING PLOT THAT LANDS TRIO IN PRISON
Mohamud allegedly discussed attacking the Mall of America with an assault rifle and told the source he could "drive straight to the crowded place and start shooting." In September, investigators say he also sent the source a selfie-style video pledging allegiance to ISIS and its leader.
The FBI then arranged an undercover weapons transaction. On Sept. 25, the source told Mohamud a "brother" could sell him an AK-style rifle, magazines and ammunition, and Mohamud allegedly indicated he wanted the weapon to be fully automatic.
On Tuesday, Mohamud met the supposed ISIS-connected "brother" — actually an undercover FBI employee — and allegedly paid $800 for an AK-47-style rifle, four magazines and roughly 200 rounds of ammunition. The rifle had been rendered inoperable, though the ammunition was live. During the meeting, Mohamud allegedly said he planned to carry out a shooting at a "kuffar festival" at the Mall of America.

Mohamud left the vehicle with the rifle, magazines and ammunition in a duffel bag and was arrested at gunpoint by FBI agents, according to the affidavit.

articles.title_orig: Rare World War II aircraft on display in Huntsville
articles.title_zh: Rare World War II aircraft on display in Huntsville
articles.content_orig:
HUNTSVILLE, Ala. ( WAFF ) - A rare piece of World War II history is in Huntsville today. The B-29 Superfortress known as Doc is at Huntsville’s airport as part of a tour stop this week.
Doc is one of only two B-29s still flying today. More than 1,600 were built in Wichita during the war.
It is joined by a P-51 Mustang. Those are rare too. Only about 150 of them are still around.
Visitors got a chance to see the aircraft up close and learn about the crews who designed, built and flew them.
“It’s a pretty special opportunity...really makes the history jump off the page,” Josh Wells said.
Wells said the event also helps younger generations understand an important piece of history.
