articles.title_orig: Parliament calls for principled EU-China policy that combines dialogue, fair trade, and human rights
articles.title_zh: Parliament calls for principled EU-China policy that combines dialogue, fair trade, and human rights
articles.content_orig:
The European Parliament has advocated establishing a stronger, more principled EU-China policy that balances dialogue with the promotion of European interests. In a recommendation approved on Wednesday by a vote of 454 in favour, 86 against, and 110 abstentions, Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) highlighted the EU’s commitment to fostering a multilateral world. They underscored the importance of engaging with China on pressing global challenges, including peace and security, climate change, and human rights.
At the same time, MEPs acknowledged that bilateral relations have reached a critical juncture, largely due to China’s unfair economic practices and its position concerning Russia’s war against Ukraine. They expressed substantial concern over verified reports indicating that the Chinese military has trained Russian military personnel for involvement in Ukraine.
MEPs contend that the EU should work closely with the United States, G7 partners, and other like-minded nations to encourage China to use its influence over Russia to help end the conflict.
“Today’s majority marks a turning point in Europe’s China policy. With this week’s Franco-German initiative, a broad EU consensus is emerging on the need for a more balanced economic relationship with China. I hope Commissioner Šefčovič will take this united economic message to Beijing tomorrow. But this report goes even further: we want cooperation with China where possible, while standing firm on our security and values. As long as fundamental differences persist, systemic rivalry will also be part of our relationship,” rapporteur Hilde Vautmans (Renew, BE) said.
Direct engagement between the European Parliament and Chinese authorities resumed last year, after a suspension that began in 2021 when the Chinese government imposed sanctions on several MEPs in response to the EU’s human rights sanctions against certain Chinese officials and organisations. Between March and June 2026, three parliamentary delegations visited China, with a fourth visit scheduled for later in October 2026.
MEPs emphasised the urgent need to address the potential risks associated with the EU’s economic dependency on China. They called for a comprehensive de-risking strategy that focuses on critical raw materials, pharmaceuticals, batteries, electric vehicles, information and communication technology, semiconductors, and other strategic sectors. The Parliament has also called for enhanced investment screening and protection of vital technologies, infrastructure, and supply chains.
Furthermore, MEPs identified several challenges facing the EU economy, such as China’s industrial overcapacity, state subsidies, and barriers limiting European firms’ access to the Chinese market. They have called for reciprocity and a level playing field in trade and investment, supporting balanced EU actions when China does not adequately open its markets. They also advocated strengthening Global Gateway partnerships to provide a credible alternative to China’s Belt and Road Initiative, especially in Africa and Latin America.
The report reaffirms the EU’s One China policy and opposes any unilateral changes to the status quo in Taiwan through force or coercion. MEPs called for heightened resilience against cyber threats, foreign interference, espionage, and hybrid challenges, while also demanding a reinforced human rights dialogue with China focused on issues such as repression, forced labour, and policies in Tibet and Xinjiang.
The Parliament expressed significant concern about the recent adoption of the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress and its potential to entrench assimilationist policies further. They also called for the unconditional release of political prisoners.

articles.title_orig: New Production of Lord of the Rings Musical to Embark on World Tour
articles.title_zh: New Production of Lord of the Rings Musical to Embark on World Tour
articles.content_orig:
This new production will be directed by Bruce Guthrie.
October 07, 2026 By Diep Tran
The road goes ever on, especially if you're a Lord of the Rings musical. A new stage production called The Lord of the Rings – The Epic Stage Adventure will world premiere at the Zorlu Performing Arts Center in Istanbul October 8, 2027. Further touring stops will include Bucharest, Prague, Warsaw, Thessaloniki, Tallinn, Athens, Sofia, Zagreb, and Dubai, with more (including venues in Europe) to be announced.
Based on J.R.R. Tolkien's fantasy novels, the new production will be directed by Bruce Guthrie, head of film and theatre at the National Centre for Performing Arts, Mumbai. It will feature scenic, video, and puppetry design by Tony and Olivier Award winner Andrzej Goulding ( Life of Pi ), and a score by Academy Award winner A.R. Rahman , the Finnish folk group Värttinä, and Tony Award Winner Christopher Nightingale, with book and lyrics by Shaun McKenna and Matthew Warchus .
It follows the hobbit Frodo as he embarks on a quest—alongside a fellowship composed of an elf, a dwarf, some men, and other hobbits—to destroy the One Ring and save Middle Earth.
The Lord of the Rings stage musical first premiered in 2006 at Princess of Wales Theatre in Toronto, before opening in the West End in 2007 at Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. A well-received production, which originated in 2023 at the Watermill Theatre in the U.K. just finished a North American and international tour. The forthcoming touring production features a new creative team.
Lord of the Rings is is produced by Kevin Wallace and William Bennett for KW Productions, George Isaak for People Entertainment Group, and Middle-earth Enterprises, LLC, with Peter Huntley and Callum Runciman as executive producers and general managers for Smart Entertainment.
Tickets for the Istanbul engagement will be available at Zorlupsm.com .
Visit LOTRmusical.com for more information.

articles.title_orig: Rubio calls for "unapologetic pursuit of national power," invoking ancient Greece in Acropolis speech
articles.title_zh: Rubio calls for "unapologetic pursuit of national power," invoking ancient Greece in Acropolis speech
articles.content_orig:
Athens — As the United States wages a costly war with Iran and Europe struggles with the grinding conflict in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood before the Acropolis on Wednesday and reached back more than two millennia to argue that the answer to the West's current problems can be found, at least in part, in ancient Greece.
In a speech timed to the sunset from the Pnyx, where Athenians gathered for their democratic assembly, Rubio cast ancient Greece as the source not only of Western democracy and philosophy, but of what he described as the character that fueled the West's rise.
"Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West," Rubio said, citing "fierce individuality and relentless ambition," and "a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory."
He argued that those modern Western societies had allowed those qualities to erode.
"The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, a world devoid of risk or failure, where neither the glory of victory, nor the shame of defeat," Rubio said. "We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre."
His remarks were delivered before roughly 250 invited guests, including senior Greek government officials, members of the diplomatic corps and representatives of the business, educational and cultural sectors, according to a senior State Department official.
The speech expanded on themes Rubio laid out at the Munich Security Conference in February, when he warned that Europe faced "civilizational erasure" and argued that the U.S. and Europe needed to recover a shared Western identity. Still, his conciliatory tone in Munich came as a relief to European officials after Vice President JD Vance had used the same stage a year earlier to sharply rebuke the continent's leaders.
In front of the Acropolis, Rubio traced the development of the West from ancient Greece through Rome, European Christianity and eventually the United States, citing Alexander the Great, Caesar, Charlemagne and Columbus along the way. He portrayed America's frontier expansion, industrial development and space program as later expressions of the same drive.
Rubio said the West now stands at a crossroads, "because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century."
"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all," he said.
"Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice," Rubio continued. "We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power, to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future."
The history Rubio presented was arguably selective. He spoke relatively little about democracy or political equality at a site closely associated with both, focusing instead on competition, national loyalty and the willingness to take risks. He argued that modern societies too often seek "perfect safety" and concern themselves more with "the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best."
"The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things," he said.
The highly produced speech came during a trip largely devoted to more immediate questions of American power: where U.S. forces can operate, how NATO allies can help counter Russia and Iran, and how American energy can displace Russian supplies in Europe.
Greece was the second stop on a three-country tour that began in Iceland and ends in Portugal on Thursday. In Iceland, amid growing U.S. attention to Arctic security, Rubio left open the possibility of an increased American military presence, saying, "We'd never do anything without cooperating with officials here about what's available. I think there is a willingness to do more together."
In Athens, Rubio met Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis for the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue, focused on defense, energy and regional security. At a news conference Wednesday, Rubio called Greece a "strong and model NATO ally," while Gerapetritis said Greece could provide maritime assistance in the Strait of Hormuz if a viable peace process is established.
Rubio was also asked by CBS News whether he was confident U.S. Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle's tenure had complied with State Department ethics rules, amid congressional scrutiny over allegations that Guilfoyle used her diplomatic position to benefit private business interests in Greece.
"This is not the format where we're going to address this," Rubio said. "Suffice it to say our embassy has been doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador." Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.
Rubio's visit and Acropolis address come at a complex moment for the Trump administration.
The U.S. is seven months into its war with Iran and has yet to secure an agreement to end it. Vice President JD Vance said this week that Iran would need to make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity, raising questions about whether the administration was backing away from its earlier insistence on zero enrichment.
Asked Wednesday by CBS News to clarify the U.S. position, Rubio declined to say what level of enrichment, if any, Washington might accept.
"I don't understand what the confusion is about the nuclear program. Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Simple, period and end of story," he said. "I'm not going to go into, you know, into the details about what would be acceptable or not."
The war has also helped push oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, adding an economic and political cost at home as the midterm elections approach.
In his remarks before the Acropolis, Rubio directly raised Iran. After invoking the Spartans at Thermopylae and Achilles' pursuit of glory at Troy, he contrasted Western ideas of sacrifice with what he called a "cult of death" among Iran's "radical mullahs."
"Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause, but they do not worship death," he said.
The speech also comes as Rubio's own political future attracts increasing attention. President Trump has publicly raised both Rubio and Vice President Vance as possible future standard-bearers for his movement.
Rubio did not overtly mention his own ambitions Wednesday, but pointed to recent administration achievements, including the Greenland deal he helped broker last month.
"It is a vision we saw in action," Rubio said, arguing the agreement would "reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO."
"We want to win together," he said. "We must win together."

articles.title_orig: World News in Brief: Child migrants in Europe, Greenland forced contraception scandal, FAO hunger updates
articles.title_zh: World News in Brief: Child migrants in Europe, Greenland forced contraception scandal, FAO hunger updates
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
New data on child migrants published on Wednesday highlighted the harrowing treatment many face while travelling to Europe in search of work and shelter.
Just over 31,000 children arrived in Greece, Italy, Spain, Bulgaria and Malta last year – 25 per cent less than in 2024.
Of more than 4,600 teenagers and young adults aged 15 to 24 surveyed, nearly half reported suffering physical violence.
One of the main routes migrants take today is the through the central Mediterranean from Libya and Tunisia in northern Africa to Italy, according to the UN migration agency, IOM .
IOM spokesperson Kennedy Omondi said there has to be stronger cooperation between European countries and those along migration routes to protect children travelling alone.
“The latest data in our report shows how vulnerable children are subjected to violence and exploitation when safe pathways are limited and they are forced to rely on smugglers,” the spokesperson said.
Among the adolescents and young adults who made the journey, 28 per cent said they had been held against their will and 17 per cent said they had been forced into work. Almost eight in 10 are male.
One 19-year-old migrant worker from Bangladesh cited in the report said his boss in Libya took away his passport and forced him into slave labour, hitting him when he was considered not to be working hard enough.
A 20-year-old woman from Liberia said she arrived in Algeria where she was raped and forced to work as a cleaner. Seven months’ pregnant, she escaped on a boat to Spain.
Most cases of abuse occurred in Libya, according to IOM. More than 20,000 of the 31,100 children who reached Europe along mixed migration routes last year arrived without a parent or guardian, according to a joint report with the UN Children’s Fund ( UNICEF ) and refugee agency, UNHCR .
IOM Director General Amy Pope called for stronger cooperation between European countries and States along migration routes to protect children travelling alone. Ms. Pope also called for action to tackle the smuggling and criminal networks that exploit them.
Independent UN human rights experts have warned that attempts to downplay the forced contraception of thousands of Inuit women and girls in Greenland threaten any prospect of genuine redress.
The concerns follow a dissenting report by two former members of an expert group appointed by Greenland’s Government.
It concluded there were no empirical grounds to assume that Danish or Greenlandic authorities intentionally and systematically inserted intrauterine devices without consent.
The two governments have already recognised that the Indigenous women and girls endured the practice for decades in public care institutions and have apologised.
But, the independent experts – who receive no salary for their work and are not UN staff – said true remedy cannot be achieved without “a clear, accurate and undisputed record of historical facts”.
They urged Denmark to make compensation schemes more accessible linguistically and culturally, ensure women with disabilities are not forgotten and address wider abuses such as forced adoption and the removal of Inuit children from their parents.
“Their dignity, voices and rights must remain at the centre of all efforts toward truth, justice, healing and reconciliation,” the Human Rights Council -appointed experts said.
The UN Food and Agriculture Organization ( FAO ) has called for urgent funding to help families in the Near East and North Africa to keep growing food and earning a living as conflict, displacement and climate pressures deepen hunger.
More than 45 million people across the region face crisis-level hunger or worse.
At the same time, funding shortfalls are limiting support to protect food production.
In Sudan, where 19.5 million people face high levels of acute food insecurity, only 23 per cent of the $193 million needed under the 2026–2028 emergency response plan has been funded. In Yemen, FAO has secured less than one per cent of the $87.9 million it requires for 2027.
In Lebanon, more than one million people were displaced after the March 2026 escalation, and more than 22 per cent of agricultural land has reportedly been damaged.
“Investing early in seeds, livestock, water and other agricultural support can protect livelihoods, prevent hunger from deepening and reduce humanitarian needs over time,” said FAO Deputy Director-General Beth Bechdol.

articles.title_orig: Asia Focus: Expanding Global Reach, World's Most Populous Continent Continues To Flourish
articles.title_zh: Asia Focus: Expanding Global Reach, World's Most Populous Continent Continues To Flourish
articles.content_orig:
Get Pollstar News and more delivered right to your inbox with Pollstar Daily Pulse.
By signing up, you agree to Pollstar’s Privacy Policy and Terms of Use
The Asian touring market continues to thrive, with promoters and venues reaping the rewards of artists both homegrown and international presenting top-notch concert productions at home and abroad, with new partnerships and long-lasting relationships behind the scenes meaning the traffic is both inbound as well as exported to the rest of the world.
The dominance of K-pop in the region, anchored by activity in Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Indonesia and Dubai, continues. The top four touring acts, as reported to Pollstar (see page 162), were K-pop bands, with SEVENTEEN showing the way with a gross of $97,394,005. TWICE grossed $76,176,781 and TOMORROW X TOGETHER did $53,035,381. Ranked No. 4, Korean powerhouse BTS grossed $49,069,994 in Asia as part of its mammoth “ARIRANG” world tour, which was No. 1 on Pollstar ’s Q3 chart. Those shows were the chart-topping boy band’s first in nearly four years due to military service.
Western acts were busy as well, with Lady Gaga leading the charge ($44,379,794 grossed), fifth overall in the territory, and Travis Scott was close behind ($37,922,441). Just to reinforce the Asian presence in the home region, G.E.M. came in seventh ($31,725,779), BLACKPINK is eighth ($29,193,966 grossed) and ENHYPEN nabbed the ninth spot ($21,562,532 grossed).
The key players in the region who Pollstar talked to were uniformly enthusiastic about business. HYBE was the leading promoter in the region with $247,965,087 in gross revenue. HYBE 360 President Yoojin Oh (Impact Honoree, see page 176), who oversees the company’s concert business, says, “Over the past year, HYBE artists’ global tours have continued to expand not only in scale but also in the breadth of markets they reach.”
Japan’s presence as the longtime leader in the Asian music industry remained strong. Three of the top five promotion agencies were Japanese and the country held six of the top 10 spots. The biggest player in the nation was Creativeman Productions, with $103,665,840 in gross revenue, third overall in Pollstar ’s Asia chart. Naoki Shimizu, president of the promoter behind the long-running Summer Sonic festival, notes, “The live music market has bounced back from the pandemic and is expanding even more than before.” Of Japan in particular, he says, “The breadth of the entertainment landscape is a key factor. There is a capacity to turn anything — whether local acts, Asian artists, Western music, anime, or voice actors — into a major live concert market.” In second place for promoters was Live Nation with $209,803,871 in gross revenue reported.
Dennis Argenzia, president of global touring, Asia-Pacific at Live Nation, has observed a shift in enthusiasm from artists. “Asia is at a really exciting point in its evolution as a live music market,” Argenzia says. “For many years, we had to convince artists and their teams to come to Asia — today, the conversation is very different. Artists want to perform here because they see the growth in demand and the opportunity to build deeper connections with fans across the region.”
Hong Kong appears as a microcosm of the expanding Asia market. The 50,000- capacity Kai Tak Stadium is a crucial venue for all of Asia. Kath Wong, senior manager at the firm that runs the stadium, emphasizes the outsized role K-pop plays in Asia touring and Hong Kong’s place in the market, with concert highlights from BLACKPINK and SEVENTEEN at Kai Tak Stadium.
“Each show serves as a milestone not only for Kai Tak Sports Park, but for Hong Kong as a whole,” Wong says. “It demonstrated that the stadium could host some of the world’s biggest touring artists and deliver complex international production to the standard expected by the artist, promoter and production teams.”
She expands on the environment, with Kai Tak Sports Park including both the 50,000-seat stadium with a retractable roof and the indoor Kai Tak Arena, which can accommodate 10,000 people and has 80% retractable seating.
Irene Chan, CEO of AsiaWorld-Expo, which operates the 14,000-cap arena of the same name in Hong Kong (the third biggest in Asia), is extremely upbeat on the business in 2026: “Audiences increasingly seek destination events that combine music, culture, fashion, art, retail, food and technology—driving the global trend of ‘festivalisation’ and creating new revenue and partnership opportunities beyond ticket sales.”
Global promoter AEG Presents, based in the U.S., is also focused on the region. Adam Wilkes, president and CEO of AEG Presents Europe and Asia-Pacific, who has worked in the Asian touring market for decades, offers a comprehensive overview.
“Asia is already a core part of the global touring ecosystem, and its significance will only grow,” he says. “International artists are reaching more markets, supported by a wave of world-class venues – both newly opened and under construction. The regional touring industry is also becoming more sophisticated, allowing artists to build meaningful careers across multiple countries rather than only at home.”
He adds that the world environment has changed, catapulting Asia to a new position. “Crucially, the traffic now moves both ways,” he says. “K-pop led the way, but Japanese, Chinese and Indian artists are increasingly finding audiences and performing at the highest level around the world. More inbound touring, better infrastructure and a growing pipeline of internationally successful Asian talent make the potential enormous.”
In Japan, Shimizu reflects on Creativeman’s successes but also looks forward.
“After Summer Sonic, the biggest tour of the year for us would be Iron Maiden,” he says of the globally renowned heavy metal pioneers. Other rock bands continue to show strength in the market. “Last year, it was Green Day, and Radiohead is coming up next year. It is a joy, after such a long career, to have tours every year by bands I’ve promoted for over two decades.”
The company is set to expand its dominant network even further. Shimizu explains, “Creativeman recently entered into a strategic partnership with AEG. In the past, artists like Taylor Swift, Justin Bieber and Ariana Grande have started out working with Creativeman for their Japan shows, only to move on to global tours handled by others. Now, however, we have a setting where we can continue working with them throughout that process. Furthermore, Creativeman’s 36 year-career will undoubtedly bring added value to AEG.”
Kaori Hayashi, president of Live Nation H.I.P. (Hayashi International Promotions), notes the promoter is set for a banner year. “We are seeing strong demand for live entertainment in Japan. More artists are touring, more live events are taking place, and more fans are attending these events. Bruno Mars’ 12-show dome tour in January 2027 will be the largest tour ever undertaken by an international artist in Japan. It will span six cities across the country – from Osaka to Nagoya – reflecting the depth of demand for international artists well beyond Tokyo, and is another indication of the scale of opportunity in this market.”
The 37,000-cap GMO Arena Saitama (formerly Saitama Super Arena), one of Japan’s biggest arenas and the second largest in Asia, has been closed for a major renovation since January. Operations will resume in April 2027, and Yutaka Minagawa, MD of the arena, tells Pollstar they have already secured a number of major international artist performances.
“Japan’s music market continues to benefit from strong and stable demand for domestic artists, particularly within the J-Pop genre,” Minagawa says. “In addition to J-Pop, K-Pop enjoys enduring popularity, while major international artists continue to include Japan as part of their world tours. This creates a highly diverse live entertainment ecosystem where multiple genres can successfully coexist.”

articles.title_orig: Paxton’s latest audio leak is making things tough for national Republicans
articles.title_zh: Paxton’s latest audio leak is making things tough for national Republicans
articles.content_orig:
by RAY LEWIS | The National News Desk
HUNT VALLEY, Md. (TNND) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the reeling Republican candidate for U.S. Senate, is blaming his so-far poor performance on factors beyond his control.
Paxton has trailed his Democratic opponent in most polls over the past few months as he struggles to attract donors wary of his legal baggage and attachment to the GOP's unpopular governance. He was charged with fraud in a since-dropped case and impeached by state Republicans, all the while defending the Trump administration's legally dubious dealings.
He told a group of donors and lobbyists at a recent closed-door event that the Iran war, and its subsequent effect on fuel prices, is more to blame for his campaign issues.
"It's the war, it's the gas prices, it's diesel," he said in an audio clip published by Axios Wednesday. "When it's over $6 a gallon for diesel ... people are feeling the pinch. So I'd say that's probably the biggest problem."
The average price for a gallon of diesel in Texas is $5.72, according to AAA data, but rates in many other states are well above $6. Many Texans are upset over fuel costs, but Paxton's legal problems also present a challenging obstacle on his road to the Senate.
Eighty-five percent of voters told The New York Times and Siena University last month they have heard of the attorney general's controversies, and 45 percent of that group said they'll consider those issues at the polls.
Paxton's spent valuable time defending himself against attacks by state Representative James Talarico, who's leaned heavily on an anti-corruption platform.
"You shouldn't believe anything a politician says, whether it's me or Ken Paxton. You should look at what we've done," Talarico said in a Fox News interview last month. "And if you look at Ken Paxton's history, he has spent his entire career enriching himself on the public's dime. I'll put my record up against Ken Paxton's every day of the week."
The National News Desk requested comment from the attorney general but hasn't received a response.
He's focused on Talarico's positions on cultural issues, which helped Republicans take control of the Senate, House and White House two years ago. The Democrat, Paxton says, is too far left for Texas's reliably red electorate.
"Texas is NOT California. James Talarico is the most radical Senate candidate our state has ever seen," Paxton said in a September call for donations. "Help us stop him before National Democrats turn Texas blue."
Do you have questions, concerns or tips? Send them to Ray at rjlewis@sbgtv.com .

Whatever Microsoft reveals at its surprise fall event, which starts on Wednesday, Oct. 7, at 10 a.m. PT (1 p.m. EST), we'll be covering it all live. The event will start on Wednesday, Oct. 7, at 10 a.m. PT (1 p.m. EST). We expect to attend follow-up sessions and demos throughout the day after the presentation.

articles.title_orig: Trump floats firing top political advisers after report they helped a pro-Russian government
articles.title_zh: Trump floats firing top political advisers after report they helped a pro-Russian government
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday distanced himself from two of his top political advisers — less than 30 days before the midterm elections — writing that if their outside work presents a conflict, “I will terminate them, immediately!”
Trump’s warning came after The New York Times published a report detailing how James Blair, one of the president’s former deputy chiefs of staff who now leads his outside political operation, and Chris LaCivita, Trump’s 2024 co-campaign manager, traveled to the Balkans last week for paid work on behalf of a pro-Russian government.
Trump was unaware that the two men had traveled to the Balkans – or that the pro-Russian government was among their clientele – until he was briefed on the impending New York Times piece, sources familiar with the situation told CNN. The president then made a series of phone calls Tuesday night asking his allies what their take on the story was, the sources said.
One source said Trump appeared annoyed, and another veteran Republican who is in touch with the president told CNN that Trump was “pissed” by the report – particularly at the revelation that the two advisers had been abroad in the home stretch of the midterm campaign, profiting off their association with him.
“Tone deaf,” the veteran Republican said of the advisers’ conduct.
But another source said Trump was simply seeking a range of opinions on what had been reported.
Trump – who has been actively campaigning for Republicans ahead of November’s midterms – ultimately decided he wanted to respond to the story, two of the sources told CNN. So on Wednesday, one of the sources said, he dictated a Truth Social post to aide Natalie Harp while in the Oval Office, commenting to those in the room that both Blair and LaCivita are outside consultants and are allowed to have other clients. One source said that at that moment, he did not seem irked.
“Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them,” Trump posted.
“I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” Trump wrote.
The president continued distancing himself from the two advisers and downplayed any conflict of interest later Wednesday. “They don’t have a conflict because they’re independent people,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
“I assume they have a lot of clients,” he went on. “So I don’t know their contract. If I thought they had a conflict … I would terminate.”
He also noted that neither currently works in the White House.
“Well they’re allowed to do that,” Trump told CNN. “They have a lot of clients and it’s okay. I’m a client over there, they have a consulting firm I guess, separately, as all people in Washington do. That’s pretty common.”
According to the Times, Blair and LaCivita traveled to Republika Srpska, a territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of elections there on Sunday. The trip came as polls show Republicans are facing severe electoral challenges in the United States.
Blair and LaCivita “were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars each through a Washington-based law firm that was retained by Republika Srpska’s government to provide counsel on voting issues,” the Times reported.
They said the work was for the government and not the nationalist party that controls it, though they are essentially one and the same.
Blair currently leads Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., and has been tasked with heading up the president’s midterm elections strategy. LaCivita is a senior adviser at MAGA Inc.
The group has been spending tens of millions of dollars trying to bolster Republican candidates ahead of the midterms, including some in reliably red territory who now appear vulnerable.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s Kevin Liptak contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Delays Threaten Funding for HIV Research
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Delays Threaten Funding for HIV Research
articles.content_orig:
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and U.S. President Donald Trump are seen in this combination of pictures created on Dec. 2, 2025.
President Donald Trump on Thursday said he is following the upcoming Brazilian election “very closely,” referring to Brazil as a “very important" country. "The people of Brazil are fantastic people,” he told reporters outside the White House. “It’s a very important election.”
The U.S. State Department later announced the suspension of its consular services in Brazil ahead of the election taking place on Sunday, citing unspecified security concerns. “U.S. citizens seeking emergency assistance during this time should not come to the Embassy, the Consulates, or other U.S. diplomatic facilities,” the security alert advised.
Brazilians are heading to the polls for a set of federal elections spanning congressional and gubernatorial races, alongside the first round of the presidential election votes. It’s set to be a decisive moment for Latin America’s largest nation, as the region has seen a shift toward the right in recent years. An Oct. 25 runoff is expected, as polls show a tight contest between leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro , who was convicted last year for plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 election loss. Trump led the conservative voices denouncing the conviction, referring to the trial as a “ witch hunt .”
While Trump has acknowledged his active interest as Brazil votes on its political future, there are concerns he could be too involved. Trump and his Administration have been accused of attempting to interfere with the high-stakes overseas election.
In a letter sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio in late September, Democratic lawmakers expressed “grave concern” over what they referred to as “the Administration’s coordinated effort to threaten our strategic alliance with Brazil and undermine the Western Hemisphere’s second-largest democracy ahead of its upcoming presidential election.”
“Over the course of President Trump’s second term, we have seen U.S. officials engage in a sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil,” the lawmakers said in the Sept. 24 letter, signed by 30 House Democrats and Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who caucuses with the Democratic Party.
In another letter sent to Rubio on Monday, three Democratic Senators voiced similar concerns about potential U.S. interference.
“This effort first escalated sharply during the summer of 2025, with the [U.S.] Administration deploying tariffs and targeted sanctions to attempt to shape the Brazilian Supreme Court’s verdict in the trial of former President Jair Bolsonaro on charges of attempting to foment a military coup to stay in power,” said the Senators, noting that the tariff pressure escalated in July this year when the Trump Administration moved to impose a new 25% tariff on many imports from Brazil—a decision labeled a “lamentable milestone” by Lula’s office.
The Senators argued that the “campaign directed at Brazil’s authorities resumed with the appointment of Darren Beattie as a senior advisor on Brazil issues in the State Department.” Beattie served as a White House speech writer in Trump’s first term, but was axed for attending a gathering of white supremacists. He returned to the fold early on in Trump’s second term. When serving as undersecretary for public diplomacy and public affairs last year, he called one of Brazil’s Supreme Court Judges a “key architect of the censorship and persecution complex directed against Bolsonaro and his supporters.”
Accusing the Trump Administration of using “diplomatic, economic, and political pressure in ways that risk weakening [Brazil’s] democratic institutions [and] undermining confidence in Brazil's electoral process,” the Senators closed the letter by asking the Administration to “commit to recognizing the certified outcome of Brazil's 2026 democratic elections.”
The White House has staunchly rejected claims of interference in Brazil’s elections.
“Conservative leaders are winning elections across the Western Hemisphere on their own merit because everyone sees the success of President Trump’s policies,” said White House spokesperson Anna Kelly in a statement to TIME. “These claims are nonsense.”
President Lula has also expressed concern over Trump’s interest in his country’s election. “I have already told President Trump it is very important that the U.S. do not interfere in Brazil’s elections,” he said in a Sept. 22 interview. “Brazilian elections are the concern of the Brazilian people. American elections are the concern of the American people.”
Lula added that he is “very worried about Marco Rubio,” claiming that the U.S. Secretary of State “is very closely connected to Bolsonaro’s people,” though he stressed that this was only “suspicion.” TIME has reached out to the State Department for comment.
Trump has not formally endorsed either candidate in Brazil’s presidential race, but his defense of former Brazilian President Bolsonaro, who was last year sentenced to 27 years in prison, is well documented.
After Trump criticized the trial proceedings as a “terrible thing” in July 2025, the Trump Administration increased pressure on Brazil’s government by imposing punishing 50% tariffs— extended in part due to Bolsonaro’s treatment in the courts—and directing the office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) to investigate trade relations with the country.
The State Department added to the pressure later that same month, when Rubio called Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes’ actions a “political witch hunt against Jair Bolsonaro” and announced visa restrictions on Moraes, unspecified judicial allies, and their immediate families.
Feliciano de Sá Guimarães, an associate professor at the Institute of International Relations at the University of São Paulo, says Lula was able to turn the economic pressure into a political argument of his own.
“Lula realized that he could play [these threats] in his favor for electoral purposes,” he says, explaining that Lula used the concept of “ rally round the flag ,” meaning that once a country is targeted by another, “the incumbent President can rally the people and say, ‘look our sovereignty is under attack.’”
The theme of sovereignty has featured prominently in Lula’s 2026 government manifesto , which points to Trump’s tariffs as damaging the Brazilian economy.
Guimarães says the U.S. Administration has since slightly altered its strategy, favoring an approach that could instead benefit Lula’s opposition.
Flávio Bolsonaro met with Trump, Rubio, and Vice President J.D. Vance at the White House in May. Trump later described the Brazilian lawmaker as a “smart young man, who loves his country very much.” Shortly after that meeting, the U.S. Administration on May 28 designated Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho—two Brazilian gangs—as terrorist organizations, with Bolsonaro appearing to take credit for the move in the media.
Guimarães says the issue may have resonated in Brazil due to public concerns about crime.
“Brazilians are so desperate with the situation of crime in the country that they are resorting to support any initiative, whether it's coming from the federal government or a foreign power to fix the problem,” Guimarães explains, so the move could be seen to strengthen Bolsonaro’s chances with the electorate.
Economic pressure has continued as well. After ordering the USTR to investigate Brazil’s trade practices last year, the office imposed 25% tariffs on the country in July under Section 301, for what it described as unfair trade practices.
Other disputes have further heightened diplomatic tensions. At the end of July, Brazil denied visas to two U.S. State Department officials, accusing them of trying to interfere in the upcoming election. Shortly afterward, Brazilian Ambassador Maria Luiza Ribeir

articles.title_orig: Merz’s conservatives in new crisis over alleged support for AfD
articles.title_zh: Merz’s conservatives in new crisis over alleged support for AfD
articles.content_orig:
This blog has now closed. Read below for a look at the latest news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 6, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Germany plans to buy four more Meko A-200 frigates from TKMS for about €5.6 million   ($6.3 billion), the Reuters news agency reported on Tuesday, citing a Finance Ministry document.
The country's parliamentary budget committee is expected to approve the purchase on Thursday, with the construction due to be finalized by 2035, as per Finance Ministry documents seen by Reuters.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius had cancelled a rival F126  frigate project with Dutch company Damen , over delays and cost overruns.
Germany’s far-right AfD party took a significant step toward exercising political power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
One month after winning 44% of the regional vote, the party secured the presidency of the state parliament, with Tobias Rausch elected as speaker of the house.
What does this moment mean for Germany? DW reports from Magdeburg.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Parliamentarians in Saxony-Anhalt have also voted for AfD politician Hans-Thomas Tillschneider to be one of the deputy speakers in the chamber.
This follows Tobias Rausch of the right-wing populist AfD being voted into the speaker's role earlier on Tuesday.
Tillschneider received 44 votes in favor in Tuesday's session, while 38 parliamentarians opposed his appointment. Nobody abstained from the vote, which was by secret ballot. The AfD has 39 seats in the chamber.
Lawmakers decided to elect three deputy speakers in total, with elections for the others expected to follow later.
Tillschneider, aged 48, is the deputy chair of the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt parliamentary group. He's an AfD veteran, having joined the party in 2013 soon after it was founded.
Tillschneider is a member of the identitarian movement, and was a member of the two AfD fringe groups — the so-called Flügel (wing) and its "Patriotic Platform" — that have since been formally disbanded. He also had close ties to the Pegida and Legida groups that organized anti-migrant protests in eastern Germany.
As well as his strong views on Islam and migration, Tillschneider is also known for his ties to Vladimir Putin's Russia. He was one of three AfD parliamentarians to visit Russia in September 2022, barely six months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine , in a visit that AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel rapidly disowned as a "private trip" and "not productive."
Since 2023, Tillschneider has written a monthly column for the Vedomosti newspaper in Russia. He attended the 73rd birthday celebrations for Putin at the Russian Embassy in Berlin last October.
The outgoing premier of Saxony-Anhalt says he can't explain where an additional four votes backing the AfD's Tobias Rausch as the state's new parliamentary speaker came from.
In a first for the far-right party, 35-year-old Rausch was elected to the post on Tuesday with the help of the populist BSW party (see entry below).
The Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group leadership had recommended that its 15 lawmakers in the state parliament abstain from voting.
But CDU regional leader and current state Premier Sven Schulze said it had become clear by this morning that not all the party's lawmakers planned to do so.
Some indicated that they planned to vote "no," Schulze said in comments to the German press agency DPA. "But none of us said we would vote 'yes,'" he added. "Not a single one."
Rausch was elected with 48 votes in favor and 29 against from 82 eligible votes in the secret ballot. There were five abstentions.
The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, meaning Rausch also got backing from members of other parties besides the AfD and BSW.
The center-left Social Democrats demanded answers, with the party's general secretary, Tim Klüssendorf, calling for the CDU to "immediately clarify who from within its ranks may have considered this disastrous decision to be right."
Klüssendorf also criticized the BSW for supporting Rausch's election.
"The BSW has made a conscious decision to elect, for the first time since 1945, a politician from a far-right party to the leadership of a German parliament," Klüssendorf told the Rheinische Post newspaper.
In addition to the CDU, the Social Democrats and the BSW, the Left party and the Greens are also represented in the state's parliament. Except for the BSW, the other parties have refused to work with the AfD, but some combination of them cast a secret vote for Rausch.
The Volksbank Köln Bonn in western Germany has agreed to part ways with a board member, Jürgen Neutgens, after a scandal over a loan he authorized to Cologne 's large brothel, Pascha.
It made the announcement on Tuesday, several months after placing Neutgens on leave and commissioning an independent law firm to investigate the transaction for potential wrongdoing.
"The investigation ... found no indications of financial irregularities or actions contravening obligations in the loan processes or the business relationship," the bank said in a press release . "Nevertheless the past weeks have weighed considerably on everyone involved."
Against this backdrop, the bank said the parties involved had mutually concluded that "a trusting and candid cooperation for the future can no longer be continued on the appropriate foundation."
It said both sides had agreed to confidentiality on the further details and terms, and thanked Neutgens for his service and wished him well for the future.
The loan was issued amid the restrictions of the COVID pandemic, which took a severe toll on the sex industry in Germany and led to the Pascha brothel in Cologne filing for insolvency and then changing ownership .
A family from China, or more specifically the autonomous casino-rich region of Macao, bought the business. But they needed a bridging loan of around €5 million (roughly $5.6 million at today's exchange rates) to cover part of the purchase price when their funds were held up in Hong Kong.
A typical German Christmas speciality intended as a gift for Pope Leo XIV was driven to Rome in an official vehicle from the state of Saxony after it was deemed unsuitable for air transport, officials revealed on Tuesday.
The 4-kilogram (8.8-pound) cake, a so-called stollen, which was made in the Ore Mountains in eastern Germany, was taken by Saxon Premier Michael Kretschmer to the Vatican for a private audience at the end of September.
The cake was reportedly too large to be taken into the cabin and too fragile to be placed in the aircraft hold, the officials said.
No information was provided on the cost by the officials at the Saxon State Chancellery.
The vehicle also transported other presents and documents.
The leader of the Green parliamentary party in Saxony-Anhalt , Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, has vowed to defend democracy following the election of a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) , Tobias Rausch, as parliamentary speaker.
The election of the member of a confirmed right-wing extremist, anti-constitutional party as house speaker meant that a "border" had been crossed, she said.
"We will not allow ourselves to be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights here or those of the people in this state are to be curtailed," she added.
Earlier in her address, she said that if the AfD were to take power in the state, her party would "speak out if people were denigrated because of their origins, beliefs or lifestyle."
Sziborra-Seidlitz said Saxony-Anhalt could not afford for "exclusion to become the political brand of this parliament and our state."
The AfD emerged from September elections as the strongest single force in parliament but has so far failed to find parties willing to enter into a coalition with it.

articles.title_orig: Nissan UK launches first ‘real-world’ driverless pilot
articles.title_zh: Nissan UK launches first ‘real-world’ driverless pilot
articles.content_orig:
Part of a government-funded research project that originated at the University of Warwick, it aims to deploy an autonomous mobility service across the U.K.
Nissan U.K.’s business unit will bring autonomous driving services to the university city of Cambridge and test its latest technology in an urban enviorment and create a blueprint to launch in other communities.
The plans are part of a government-funded research project backed by Nissan that launched in September 2023 at the University of Warwick with the goal of deploying an autonomous mobility service across the U.K.
The pilot trial, dubbed “ADventure,” will be coordinated between the automaker, local authorities, commuters and residents, the company said in its Sept. 28 release .
Using a specially adapted 2022 Nissan Leaf electric vehicle , the project hopes to focus on how future AD technology “can create social value, improve accessibility and address local transport challenges,” Nissan said.
The automaker used the common example of elderly people in the U.K. having to travel to a medical appointment when they do not drive themselves.
Nissan will draw on more than a decade of research by its engineers at the Nissan Technical Center Europe, which will lead the autonomous mobility project.
By choosing the driving environment in Cambridge for the automaker’s first real-world trial, Nissan aims to create a blueprint that it can refine and replicate across the U.K.
“This project is an important step for autonomous mobility in the UK,” said David Moss, SVP research and development for Nissan vehicles across the Africa, Middle East, India, Europe and Oceania regions. “With UK Government backing, it will take autonomous vehicle research beyond central London and into another city, helping us understand how these services can work for different communities and real-life journeys.”
“By developing and applying Nissan’s in-house expertise, combined with the wider knowledge from our partners, we can delve further into how self-driving vehicles can improve connectivity, accessibility and quality of everyday life,” Moss added.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.title_zh: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.content_orig:
Chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in Antarctica down by two-thirds since 2011, probably due to climate crisis
The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed.
Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica , increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, Prof Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey .
The Guardian revealed in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem.
The new study, published on Wednesday in Current Biology, indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird – which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek – may need to be classified as an endangered species.
The island of Zavodovski had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic peninsula to 5C above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4C, about 20C above normal for the time of year – a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy”.
Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the north-west of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30% – though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.
after newsletter promotion
He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”
The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.
Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “Penguin Pompeii hypothesis” of a sudden population fall , this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.

articles.title_orig: Students at Lincoln University, an HBCU, Sue Missouri for $549 Million, Citing Funding Disparities
articles.title_zh: Students at Lincoln University, an HBCU, Sue Missouri for $549 Million, Citing Funding Disparities
articles.content_orig:
Lincoln University students and alumni filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the state of Missouri on Wednesday, alleging decades of unequal funding between it and the University of Missouri.
The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri and is the first case brought by the 1890 Project challenging a state allegedly failing to appropriately fund an 1890 land-grant university, according to the plaintiffs' lawyers.
The 1890 Project monitors promises made in the federal government's second Morrill Act in 1890, which aimed to ensure historically Black universities were equitably funded as certain white universities had been through the original 1862 Morrill Act.
These land-grant institutions were supposed to be provided funding for programs to strengthen research, extension and teaching, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture .
The New York Times reported that between 1987 and 2020 , federal officials found Missouri appropriated $361.6 million less to Lincoln on a per-student basis than to the University of Missouri.
The students and alumni are seeking a court-ordered remedy to combat the alleged disparity and permanently require that Missouri fully match Lincoln's federal land-grant funding.
They also allege that the funding disparity stems from the University of Missouri being founded in 1839 for white students and Lincoln University being separately designated as a land-grant institution in 1890 for Black students.
The University of Missouri is an 1862 land-grant university , established under different legislation than the 1890 land-grant universities.

Lincoln students and alumni, as well as their lawyers, spoke on the lawsuit at a press conference at 11 a.m. Wednesday at the Missouri State Capitol Rotunda.
The 1890 Project wrote that in Sept. 2023, the U.S. secretaries of agriculture and education documented more than $12 billion in funding shortfalls across 16 states.
These were measured between 1987 and 2020 and compared to each state's 1862 land-grant university.
The lawsuit's defendants include the Coordinating Board for Higher Education, Gov. Mike Kehoe, Commissioner of Higher Education and Workforce Development Bennett Boggs, and UM System President Mun Choi.
The plaintiffs include one alumni, a former student and four currently enrolled Lincoln University students, according to court documents.
Lincoln University had no comment on this case as of Wednesday morning.

articles.title_orig: Trump claims world’s lowest drug prices. TrumpRx discounts a ‘mixed bag,’ report shows.
articles.title_zh: Trump claims world’s lowest drug prices. TrumpRx discounts a ‘mixed bag,’ report shows.
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, President Donald Trump has increasingly touted his drug pricing deals, claiming the U.S. is now paying the world’s lowest prescription drug prices. “This one thing alone should win us the midterms,” he recently said at the White House.
TrumpRx.gov, the public face of his drug pricing discounts, has grown dramatically since its launch in February. What started as a few dozen brand-name drugs now includes a catalog of more than 800 brand-name and generic medications, offering discounts on everything from popular weight loss drugs to treatments for cancer and rheumatoid arthritis.
It’s unclear whether the average American has “ saved a fortune,” as Trump promised .
Prescription drug prices fell by 3.1% over the year ending in July, according to federal inflation data — though experts say it’s too soon to know how much of the drop, if any, can be attributed to Trump’s drug pricing deals. The site has relied on GoodRx’s pricing data and technology to power many of its listings and blends pre-existing discounts from drugmakers with newly negotiated prices.
At the Republican midterm convention last month , Trump said, “We went from the highest prescription drug prices, by far, anywhere in the world, to the lowest prescription drug prices anywhere in the world.”
A recent analysis from KFF finds that TrumpRx prices are competitive with prices in other countries for a small number of cancer and cholesterol medications. In many cases, Americans aren’t getting the best deals compared with the rest of the world.
Take Ozempic. For the average patient in the U.S. paying out of pocket, the blockbuster diabetes drug can cost $349 to more than $1,000 a month. It’s $349 through TrumpRx. Yet in several other wealthy countries, the next-highest price is $190 a month, according to KFF, a nonpartisan research group.
Enbrel is an even starker example. A monthly supply of the rheumatoid arthritis drug costs $3,354 through TrumpRx, more than five times the $641 average in the other countries where researchers found prices.
Some drugs, however, come out well ahead. Rydapt, a drug used to treat certain blood cancers, costs $2,909 for 56 capsules through TrumpRx — less than half the $5,901 price for the same amount in France, the next-cheapest country.
Those disparities run throughout the site, according to the KFF analysis. The report, which didn’t compare TrumpRx savings within the U.S., offers one of the first broad worldwide comparisons of Trump’s drug pricing claims.
The analysis looked at 32 brand-name drugs sold through TrumpRx that lacked generic or biosimilar equivalents. Researchers focused on those drugs because patients don’t have the option of switching to cheaper versions, meaning the discounts offered through TrumpRx could have a greater impact on what they pay.
The group compared the prices with those in 11 other wealthy countries, including Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. The prices are current as of Aug. 26.
The results were almost evenly split. For 17 of the drugs, the TrumpRx prices were lower than the average prices abroad. For 15, they were higher. But Trump has promised Americans the lowest prices in the world. By that measure, the results were less favorable: Only five were actually the lowest-priced, while 13 were the highest-priced.
“It’s kind of a mixed bag,” said Juliette Cubanski, deputy director of the Medicare policy program at KFF, who co-authored the report. “Even with the reductions that may have been agreed to by manufacturers who are listing their drugs on the TrumpRx website, the prices that they’re offering, even at a discount, still continue to be higher than prices in comparable countries.”
The findings offer an early look at both the promise and the limits of Trump’s approach to lowering drug prices.
Americans routinely pay more for prescription drugs than patients in other wealthy countries, even when the medications are made by the same companies. The TrumpRx discounts, the White House says, stem from Trump’s “ most favored nation ” pricing deals, agreements with drugmakers to charge Americans the lower prices they offer other countries in exchange for tariff relief. But the discounts can vary widely, the analysis found, and they haven’t consistently produced the lowest prices Trump promised.
“I’m not surprised by these findings,” said Dr. Benjamin Rome, a primary care physician and health policy researcher at Harvard Medical School. “Any of us who have been following drug prices realized, as soon as TrumpRx was launched, it was a limited number of drugs and it was clear that the prices that were there were not always going to be linked or in any way related to what the prices are in other countries.”
It’s a markedly different approach from the one taken by Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden.
Rather than use Medicare’s power to negotiate prices for a limited number of costly drugs each year, TrumpRx relies largely on voluntary agreements with individual drugmakers to offer discounted prices directly to consumers. (The exact details of the agreements remain largely confidential, and the White House has declined to disclose them.)
TrumpRx doesn’t sell the drugs directly. For many drugs, it sends consumers to manufacturer programs through which they can obtain coupons or discounted cash prices without insurance.
That’s not how most people get their prescription drugs. About 9 in 10 Americans have some form of health insurance , meaning many pay for medications through private insurance, Medicare or Medicaid — although discounted cash-pay options have become increasingly popular as insurance has gotten more expensive. The money spent on TrumpRx doesn’t count toward a patient’s copay or deductible.
“They’re highly selected products where the manufacturer is willing to offer a discount,” Rome said. “Maybe they’re not the products causing the highest spending in the U.S. in some cases or are products where they were already offering confidential discounts, but now they’re making those discounts more public.”
The site now includes several cheaper, generic medications. “But those generics and the low prices for those generics pre-existed the TrumpRx website ,” Cubanski said.
The KFF analysis doesn’t capture every drug available through TrumpRx, and there are limits to how much can be concluded from it.
Antonio Ciaccia, CEO of 46brooklyn Research, a group that tracks drug pricing in the U.S., counts about 80 brand-name drugs currently on TrumpRx, while KFF was able to compare prices for 32.
Part of the challenge, Ciaccia said, is that some drugs sold in the U.S. aren’t available in all of the countries KFF examined. That can make direct comparisons difficult.
“One of the big differences is the U.S. market does have more products in it than international markets, so that is noteworthy to the extent we have options here in the U.S. rather than a one-size-fits-all treatment approach,” he said.
International prices aren’t always perfectly comparable, either, he said. The analysis relied on publicly available prices, which may not include confidential discounts negotiated between foreign governments and drugmakers.
Ciaccia also noted that KFF’s 11 comparison countries don’t exactly match the countries used in some of the administration’s international pricing programs.
A White House spokesperson referred NBC News to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services for comment. The CMS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Those limitations don’t change the basic comparison at the heart of Trump’s claim: whether the prices offered to Americans match or beat those available abroad.
“We wanted to put that claim to the test with this analysis,” Cubanski said. “There is not a clear pattern across the board for higher prices or no consistent pattern across the board for lower prices. ”

articles.title_orig: Three years after Oct. 7, Israeli strikes in Gaza grind on and deaths climb
articles.title_zh: Three years after Oct. 7, Israeli strikes in Gaza grind on and deaths climb
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani released a statement on the three-year anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks in Israel.
Mamdani faces renewed scrutiny over his views on the war. He has condemned the Oct. 7 attacks while also sharply criticizing Israel's response and describing it as a genocide.
His statement on Wednesday said the suffering did not begin nor end that day, and "it has continued through Israeli government's devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers. It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7. On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others. We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss. The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government's devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians—including more than 21,000 children. Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed. That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing. Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them - all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes. Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment. To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity."
It is Mamdani's first Oct. 7 anniversary as mayor, and his planned appearances throughout the day are expected to draw close attention from both supporters and critics.
The attack by Hamas killed nearly 1,200 people and resulted in 251 hostages being taken. Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza has resulted in thousands of Palestinian deaths.
The ADL released a statement in response to Mamdani's and accused him of "weaponizing a day meant for mourning."
"@NYCMayor, not once do you say 'Jews.' On Oct. 7, Hamas-led attackers murdered civilians, committed sexual violence, mutilated bodies and took hostages. You are weaponizing a day meant for mourning the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust to recycle your usual antizionist talking points. The city with the largest Jewish population outside Israel deserves a mayor who can honor the dead without exploiting them."
The Israeli Consulate, which had invited Mamdani to view Oct. 7 footage in the days leading up to the anniversary, issued a fiery statement that said in part:
"The mayor's statement is a disgrace, shame, and insult to the memory of those who were murdered on October 7. It is still not too late to attend our screening this evening of the October 7 footage and see with your own eyes, for the first time, the monsters you support," Amb. Ofir Akunis said.
Akunis said "anyone with a heart" should be ashamed of Mamdani's response.
"Mamdani, displaying a shocking lack of basic humanity, continues to spread antisemitic blood libels against the Jewish state. New York City should be appalled that its mayor shows such contempt for the memory of those who were murdered," Akunis concluded.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Retreat: From the Gulf to Britain, American Forces Pull Back
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Retreat: From the Gulf to Britain, American Forces Pull Back
articles.content_orig:
British police on Tuesday arrested a 22-year-old man in London on suspicion of a terror offense over a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that authorities have linked to Iran. It was the seventh arrest in connection with a suspected plot against RAF Fairford , 100 miles west of London, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran during the ongoing war.
The U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing force said the man, a British national, was detained in the Westminster area of central London on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.
The six other men who were arrested as part of the investigation have been released on bail, under investigation and monitoring. The decision to bail them drew criticism last week from President Trump .
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said detectives "continue to pursue multiple lines of enquiry" and "remain committed to investigating all possible angles."
Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base early on Sept. 27 as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swooped on the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline —   in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the U.K. sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident, without saying why or what the nature of the suspected plot was.
Mr. Trump had previously said Iran "might be" involved, telling reporters on Sept. 28 that U.S. and British authorities worked "very closely" on the matter and "we know everything about them. We would not have released them" from custody.
Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
The U.S. moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford on Sunday, though it's unclear whether or how the move was connected to the arrests. Mr. Trump told reporters on Monday he didn't want to tempt "the enemy" by having the bombers there.
"We had a threat, and if we're going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that," he said in Washington, adding that the people behind the unspecified threat "would be linked to Iran," without offering details.

articles.content_orig:
These include a lock, a thermostat and a temperature sensor.
A recent report indicated that Apple and LG have teamed up to develop several smart home gadgets, with an official reveal expected next week . Now, a reputable leaker has posted several renders of these gadgets, along with some specifications.
These leaked images feature the smart lock, thermostat and temperature sensor. The LG Smart Deadbolt Lock looks to have a keypad that rotates to open. It reportedly supports automatic unlocking and tap to unlock, with integrated emergency power and master codes. The leaker says it ships with two mechanical keys.
Here's your first look at home accessories Apple has co-developed with LG. 🧵
• The keypad rotates to open. You can use the included swivel pin to limit the rotation on one side so it doesn't touch a wall. • Settings for Touchpad Light Ring, Door... pic.twitter.com/Gy8CFXvc1F
— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 7, 2026
The LG Smart Thermostat includes settings for humidity, brightness and language. As for the design, it looks pretty much like every other smart thermostat out there. It's circular and, you know, thermostat-shaped.
The LG Temperature Sensor can also sense humidity and features a magnetic back for attaching to metal surfaces. It ships with a replaceable battery.
• Temperature and humidity sensing. • The sensor has a magnetic back to attach to metal surfaces. Comes with a metal plate with adhesive for attaching to other surfaces. • Replaceable battery and replacement alerts. pic.twitter.com/MCsBbtiBie

These aren't the only three smart home devices that the two companies are likely cooking up. Reporting suggests that Apple and LG are also working on a video doorbell, an indoor camera, an outdoor camera and a floodlight camera. All of these gadgets will reportedly launch under the LG branding, and not as Apple products.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest steam locomotive returns to the rails for special holiday tour
articles.title_zh: World’s largest steam locomotive returns to the rails for special holiday tour
articles.content_orig:
For the first time since 2019, Union Pacific’s Living Legend No. 844 will be hitting the rails with Big Boy No. 4014. These historic locomotives will be together for a special holiday tour this November.
On November 21, the pair of steam locomotives will run during a fundraising tour from Greeley to Denver, Colorado. The trip will benefit the Make-A-Wish Foundation, with a donation from Union Pacific’s Community Ties Giving Program. The steam duo will also be on display to the public at Denver’s Union Station. Santa Claus and his elves will even be in the terminal handing out limited-edition gifts. Admission to this event is free and open to the public.
Tickets for the holiday fundraising tour to take a ride in vintage passenger cars pulled by Big Boy and No. 844 go on sale to patrons of the Union Pacific Railroad Museum on October 16. The general public can purchase any remaining tickets on October 19. Families can still visit Denver’s Union Station to view the locomotives free of charge.
Nicknamed the “Living Legend,” No. 844 is a famed high-speed passenger locomotive . It was built in 1944 and the last steam locomotive built for Union Pacific. It hauled some of the company’s most recognizable passenger trains, including the Overland Limited, Los Angeles Limited, Portland Rose, and Challenger . No. 844 is also the last Class I North American steam locomotive and never permanently retired from service. Instead, it was reassigned to freight service in Nebraska from 1957 to 1959, when diesel locomotives took over passenger service duties. Unlike nearly every other steam locomotive of its era, No. 844 escaped the scrap yard in 1960 and Union Pacific retained it for special service.
No. 844 will chug alongside a more famous locomotive, Big Boy No. 4014. Big Boy is currently the world’s largest operating steam locomotive and one of only eight remaining Big Boys in existence and the only one still in operation. These powerful locomotives were constructed during World War II to transport heavy equipment to support the war effort.
Earlier this year, Big Boy drew millions of spectators during a coast-to-coast journey celebrating the United States’ 250th birthday . The first leg began on March 29. Big Boy then traveled to several states including California, Utah, and New York.
The steam locomotive celebrated the Fourth of July in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania , where the Declaration of Independence was written in 1776. Thousands of train enthusiasts braved temperatures of 102 degrees Fahrenheit (with a real-feel of 112 degrees) to catch a glimpse of the 133-foot-long and 1.2-million-pound train.
