articles.title_orig: IceCube, high-energy neutrinos, and Francis Halzen win 2026’s Physics Nobel
articles.title_zh: IceCube, high-energy neutrinos, and Francis Halzen win 2026’s Physics Nobel
articles.content_orig:
Credit : Bryce Richter / UW–Madison
An astrophysics column on big questions and our universe.
There’s a whole entire Universe out there, and the more we learn about it as it actually is, the greater our potential becomes to achieve great things as a civilization, even if the path from knowledge to improving humanity is far from clear. The Nobel Prize was set up more than 100 years ago with the express purpose of rewarding those whose work provides the “greatest benefit to humankind” in a number of disciplines, including physics. We couldn’t foresee that:
Similarly, we cannot know what advances will arise in the future from advances made today in fields like elementary particle physics, gravitational waves, or neutrino astronomy, but possibilities range from computational advances to superior timekeeping technologies to extraterrestrial communication. One thing is certain, however: we have to make the fundamental advance, first, if we ever hope to find out. In many ways, that’s what the science of physics is all about.
It’s for that reason that the world ought to be incredibly excited that the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics has gone to Francis Halzen , for “decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” which is a remarkable testament to what a single individual can accomplish with a creative idea, a lot of hard work and organization, persistence, a strong national investment in science, and quite a bit of good luck. Here’s the story of this remarkable advance in neutrino physics and astrophysics.
The idea of IceCube was born 39 years ago, back before “neutrino astrophysics” was a field that went beyond our Solar System. Prior to 1987, neutrino astrophysics was restricted solely to measuring the neutrinos coming from within the Solar System: by building a large tank of fluid deep underground. Starting in 1968 , the idea was that neutrinos from the Sun, occasionally, would interact with an atomic nucleus, transmuting a neutron into a proton, and converting the neutrino into an electron in the process. By looking for the newly transmuted nuclei, solar neutrinos could then be detected.
In principle, nuclear reactions would occur all across the Universe, releasing neutrinos when they did, but the flux would be far too low to detect them. However, due to contemporaneous interest in grand unified theories , particle physicists had begun building much larger tanks of fluid surrounded by photomultiplier tubes, with the idea being to detect any spontaneously decaying protons by measuring their faster-than-light in the liquid medium radiation: Cherenkov radiation .
The major experiment of the 1980s, Kamiokande , was originally an experiment to search for nucleon decay in Kamioka, Japan. Running for several years, it only obtained null results, until the day of February 24, 1987. All of a sudden, an array of signals emerged: 12 of them (antineutrinos, technically) in the Kamiokande II detector alone . Four hours later, the light arrived as well, confirming this was indeed a supernova event. Kamiokande, the Kamioka nucleon decay experiment, kept the same acronym, but renamed itself to the Kamioka neutrino detector experiment. From a failed search for proton decay , the science of neutrino astronomy was born.
Over the subsequent years and decades, most approaches to neutrino detection simply scaled up this approach. Large, underground, liquid-filled detectors lined with photomultiplier tubes optimized to detect Cherenkov radiation were the key to building neutrino detectors, including Super-Kamiokande and the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNOLab), where the original research led to a Nobel Prize awarded in 2002 for neutrino physics and the upgraded research led to one in 2015 for neutrino oscillations.
However, in the aftermath of the 1987 supernova and subsequent neutrino detection, Francis Halzen began thinking about a different approach. Giant tanks were fundamentally limited in a key way: the effective volume available for interactions with neutrinos was constrained to be no larger than the size of your tank. If you wanted to find rare events, your only options were to either build a larger tank or to wait for longer periods of time, until such a neutrino from a rare event happened to interact within your detector.
Halzen came up with an alternative in 1988, which he merely (and humbly) referred to as a “cute idea,” which was to do away with a photomultiplier tube-lined tank entirely. Instead, he wondered, given that there’s so much ice located at the Earth’s south pole, could one simply use Antarctic ice as the “detector” for interacting with neutrinos instead?
Of course, it wouldn’t be possible or practical to use the entire Antarctic ice sheet, but Halzen realized that if you restricted yourself to a mere section of it — a large, cubical block — you could vastly increase the potential interaction volume over what you could ever hope to build with a conventional, liquid-filled and photomultiplier tube-lined detector. If it could be implemented successfully, Halzen’s vision could bring about a neutrino detector that was able to see events that were far rarer than the other neutrino detector designs would be sensitive to.
We had a longstanding hint of this from cosmic rays: non-neutrino particles (mostly protons, but also some heavier nuclei) that struck and interacted with Earth’s upper atmosphere, producing energetic particle showers. Sometimes, the daughter particles emerging from the shower could be detected directly on the ground, but most frequently, the shower of particles would interact with the Earth’s atmosphere: moving faster-than-light in the medium of air, and producing a cone of blue light that was once again the hallmark of Cherenkov radiation. Arrays of Cherenkov telescopes routinely detect this light, and reconstruct the signatures (and energies) of the particles that originally created them. When they do, they find that there are cosmic particles out there far, far more energetic than anything we could ever hope to realistically produce in laboratory experiments here on Earth.
If these high-energy particles — albeit, rare particles — are out there in the Universe, ostensibly created by high-energy sources like neutron stars, black holes, and active quasars, then it stands to reason that similar processes will create ultra-energetic neutrinos as well. However, since the number of particles above a given energy rapidly decreases as a function of energy, it would also imply that ultra high-energy neutrino events should be exceedingly rare as well, requiring enormous volumes of “detector material” in order to even see one or a few of them.
Super-Kamiokande is the world’s largest operational neutrino detector tank, holding just over 50,000 tonnes of extraordinarily pure water, but is only about 40 meters on a side. (Technically, in a cylindrical shape.) For comparison, however, if you went deep into the Antarctic ice, you should be able to find ice that is:
Halzen’s idea was to use hot water to bore cylindrical holes straight down into the Antarctic ice at regularly spaced intervals, and then to place specialized Cherenkov detectors down deep within the ice itself, filling the gaps back up with water to restore the ice back to its pristine, block-like state. If these detectors were spaced out over a volume of ice that was a cubic kilometer in size — 1 km × 1 km × 1 km — it would possess 20,000 times the detection volume of Super-Kamiokande!
The prototype for what would become the IceCube neutrino detector was known as AMANDA: the Antarctic Muon And Neutrino Detector Array . AMANDA was made up of optical modules — each with one photomultiplier tube inside to be sensitive to Cherenkov light — that were sunk into the Antarctic ice beneath the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. By the time AMANDA-II was developed, it was scaled up to be an array of 677 modules across 19 se

articles.title_zh: World Clean-up Day 2026: Community action for cleaner and more resilient communities - International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.source: International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.content_orig:
On 19 September 2026, the ReSea Women Influencers, Gizela Lucilia and Onésia Mazelete, joined the ReSea team and community focal points in a clean-up campaign across Vilankulo, Mozambique bringing together community groups, local institutions, civil society organisations and students in a shared commitment to a cleaner environment.
World clean-up day in Vilankulo, Mozambique by ReSea women influencers.
World clean-up day in Vilankulo, Mozambique by ReSea women influencers.
World clean-up day in Vilankulo, Mozambique by ReSea women influencers.
The initiative focused on the Vilankulo Municipal Market and other locations within the municipality, combining practical cleanup activities with environmental awareness on responsible waste management, cleaner public spaces and the importance of community participation in reducing pollution.
This collective effort brought together representatives from the Municipality of Vilankulo, the Associação Juvenil Para o Desenvolvimento Comunitário (AJUPADEC), the Youth Action for Climate Action Mozambique (YACAC-Moz), the Higher School of Rural Development (ESUDER), ParCo, and pupils from local primary and secondary schools. The ReSea team was represented by Gizela Lucilia, Onésia Mazelete, Anselmo Nhanenge and Elcídio Cossa, alongside community focal points Ivanilde and Joalina.
For the ReSea Women Influencers, participation in World Cleanup Day is an important part of their commitment to environmental stewardship and community engagement. Through initiatives such as this, they continue to strengthen their role in environmental awareness, community mobilisation and the protection of coastal communities.
Activities such as World Cleanup Day also reinforce the broader objectives of ReSea, particularly community engagement, environmental stewardship and the protection of coastal communities and ecosystems from pollution.
Cleaner and more resilient communities depend on sustained local action. In Vilankulo, this means bringing communities, institutions and young people together to take shared responsibility for the spaces and ecosystems on which they depend.
The Regenerative Seascapes for People, Climate and Nature (ReSea) Project is a multi-million dollar initiative funded by Global Affairs Canada under the Partnering for Climate engagement. Co-implemented by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and Mission inclusion, the project aims to enhance the physical, social, and economic climate resilience of vulnerable coastal communities, particularly women and youth.

articles.title_orig: Russian Plague Scare: WHO Seeks Details About Reported Second Illness As Trump Plans Putin Call
articles.title_zh: Russian Plague Scare: WHO Seeks Details About Reported Second Illness As Trump Plans Putin Call
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the pneumonic plague , after the death of a female staffer at a Russian anti-plague lab that’s sparked public health fears worldwide.
Asked whether he had spoken with Putin about the matter, Trump told reporters on the White House South Lawn that he had a “call scheduled” and that it would take place “very soon.”
The Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s remarks.
Trump had told reporters Monday that he was willing to help Russia, calling the pneumonic plague “a rough disease.”
“I hate to see them having it,” Trump said. “Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we’re always willing to help.”
A Russian health watchdog said last week that Darya Shipilova, 28, a staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, had died from a “pneumonia of undetermined” origin.
The watchdog concluded that plague was not found among the staffer’s contacts, saying only that they found two cases of Covid and one of rhinovirus.
A State Department official told NBC News earlier Tuesday that the U.S. had been in contact with the Russian government regarding the incident since as early as Friday, following reports of Shipilova’s death.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Russia should share more information with the world, but asked the public not to jump to conclusions.
“Maybe, you know, there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” Rubio told reporters during a news conference in Iceland. “But I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate about what this might or might not be or what this is or what this isn’t.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday it was aware of and monitoring reports of the death, which it called “a suspected case of pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia.”
“At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC wrote on X .
Raquel Coronell Uribe is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Former German intelligence chief arrested on espionage charges
articles.title_zh: Former German intelligence chief arrested on espionage charges
articles.content_orig:
The man who led Germany’s intelligence agency from 1998 to 2005 has been arrested on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason, according to the country’s federal prosecutor’s office.
The office announced on Tuesday that August Hanning, 80, was arrested and faces charges including “treasonous espionage, obtaining state secrets, attempted treason” through contact with foreign intelligence services.
The office has not specified which country or countries Hanning is accused of working for.
Citing unnamed sources, however, German news outlet Der Spiegel reported that Hanning was in contact with an Azerbaijan intelligence agency representative. In 2025, prosecutors also accused Hanning of ties with Israeli spies in a separate case which ultimately led them to the ex-intelligence boss’s alleged espionage for other agencies.
If found guilty, treason carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment in Germany.
German news outlet Deutsche Welle described Hanning’s arrest as Germany’s “biggest espionage scandal of the century”.
Born in Nordwalde, Westphalia, western Germany, in 1946, Hanning served as the head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and later moved to work in the Federal Ministry of the Interior, before working as a state secretary until 2009.
He later worked as a private consultant.
German media showed pictures of Hanning being taken from his red-brick house in Norwalde, close to Munster, to a bulletproof vehicle by masked officers on Tuesday morning.
They claim Hanning used classified intelligence to “draft an analysis” for a foreign intelligence service and kept “close contact” with another foreign spying service for “several years” while he was working as a private consultant.
They say that in 2010, Hanning came to an agreement to receive confidential information from his former bureau chief – who was in office until March this year and is named only as “Manfred D” – and was preparing to provide an “analysis” of it to a foreign power in exchange for money. It is unclear if the analysis was duly shared.
However, Hanning is also alleged to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, partly based on information provided by Manfred D, to a contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service.
Manfred D was also arrested on Tuesday and charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
“Both suspects are believed to have agreed, in the spring of 2010, to have Manfred D continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the Federal Intelligence Service to Hanning in exchange for remuneration,” a statement from the prosecutor’s office said.
Over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, “many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings”, it added.
“Hanning was to capitalise on said information in the context of his private consulting services, which he had since been offering,” the prosecutor’s office said.
The alleged espionage by Hanning and Manfred D was uncovered during an investigation into a separate kidnapping case involving German businesswoman and steakhouse chain heiress, Christina Block.
In that case, Hamburg prosecutors accused Block of arranging the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Prosecutors said Hanning put Block in touch with a private Israeli espionage firm to carry out the abductions. The former spy chief and a police officer were accused of accepting more than 100,000 euros ($112,000) from Block in exchange for returning her children from Denmark, where they were living with her ex-husband. The trial is ongoing.
Little detail is available about the contents of the 2,000 documents, but German news outlet Suddeutsche Zeitung reported that a number of them related to Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian military.
It added that other materials were highly sensitive and classified as secret by allied intelligence agencies in other countries.
Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said in a statement to the AFP news agency that Berlin would not “tolerate the betrayal of secrets”.
“Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out,” he said, adding that Hanning’s alleged actions would amount to “trampling his official duties underfoot”.
The current head of the BND, Martin Jaeger, told the German Rheinische Post newspaper that the agency had “quickly carried out extensive internal investigations” into the former chief before federal prosecutors took over the case.
“For the BND and for me, there are no compromises when it comes to internal security,” Jaeger said, adding that it had “not called into question any of my aims or any of my priorities”.
In 2023, a high-ranking German intelligence officer, identified as “Carsten L”, was charged with high treason when prosecutors alleged he had obtained classified intelligence on the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and shared it with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). His case is ongoing.
In 1974, West German Chancellor Willy Brandt was forced to resign following revelations that an East German spy had worked as his close aide for nearly two years.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures little changed after S&P 500 hits fresh record: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures little changed after S&P 500 hits fresh record: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures inched lower early Wednesday after the S&P 500 reached a fresh all-time intraday high and a record close in the previous session, driven by a tech stock rally.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were down 0.09%, while S&P 500 futures were flat and Nasdaq-100 futures were down 0.21%.
In trading on Tuesday, the S&P 500 gained 0.58%, marking its fourth positive session in a row and closing above a level of 7,800 for the first time. The Dow gained 0.49%, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.45%.
Chipmakers were the big winners on Tuesday, with Marvell Technology gaining 5.8% on higher revenue guidance and Advanced Micro Devices climbing 2.8% after Citi hiked its price target, citing rising demand for central processing units.
Bond yields took a break on Tuesday from the steady march upward they began at the end of February, coinciding with the start of the U.S.-Israel war on Iran. Treasury yields moved higher on Wednesday ahead of a closely watched 10-year note auction .
Investors warned Tuesday about falling foreign demand for U.S. debt amid geopolitical pressures.
"The Chinese don't want to continue to accumulate," investor Ray Dalio told Bloomberg. "When you have a debtor-creditor relationship and you have an adversary relationship, that's a very difficult dynamic."
Investors are awaiting the minutes of the Federal Reserve's last meeting in September, at which the U.S. central bank raised interest rates for the first time since 2023. Minutes are set to shed light on how monetary policymakers are thinking about economic conditions.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 0.92% lower as the broader Topix fell 0.7%. South Korea's Kospi declined nearly 2%, while the small-cap Kosdaq lost 2.34%. Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 ended flat. The mainland China market remained closed for the Golden Week holiday.
Shares listed in Europe opened broadly lower on Wednesday, with the regional Stoxx 600 index down 0.4% shortly after the bell.
Average house prices in the U.K. were flat in September, according to data from lender Lloyds , after falling 0.3% the previous month.
The average property price in the country is now £298,441 ($395,005), compared to £298,395 in August. The index was also flat on an annual basis.
"While the market overall has been fairly subdued, property prices have so far proved resilient during a period of higher mortgage rates, which has been driven by changing expectations around the future path of Base Rate," Andrew Asaam, mortgages director at Lloyds, said in the data release. "That's mirrored in wider economic data, with household spending holding up better than many expected despite energy and other cost pressures arising from the Middle East conflict."
Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 0.92% lower at 70,035.71, and the broader Topix fell 0.70% to 4,154.11.
South Korea's Kospi declined nearly 2% to 6,803.90, while the small-cap Kosdaq lost 2.34% to 898.43.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 ended flat at 8,727.70.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was down 0.50% as of its last hour of trade on Wednesday. Mainland China market remained closed for the Golden Week holiday.
Shares listed in Europe opened broadly lower on Wednesday, with the regional Stoxx 600 index down 0.4% shortly after the bell.
Mining and tech stocks led losses, while Germany's DAX — down 0.9% — notched the biggest decline among major regional bourses.
Yields on bonds issued by various governments moved higher on Wednesday morning, amid lingering economic concerns.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury was up 4 basis points to 5.309% as of 2:30 a.m. ET. Yields on the longer-maturity 30-year Treasury note added almost 5 basis points to 5.688%.
Bond yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Yields on U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, also rose across the curve, with 10- and 20-year bond yields rising by 5 basis points.
Meanwhile, French and Italian 10-year government bond yields rose by 8 basis points. Japanese bonds bucked the trend, with yields trading marginally lower.
NLFI, a non-profit organization that manages shares of nationalized or bailed-out financial institutions owned by the Dutch state, said Wednesday that it would sell part of its stake in lender ABN Amro.
The sale would be carried out through a pre-arranged trading plan, executed by BofA Securities Europe, it said. Once completed, it would reduce NLFI's holding of ABN Amro to a 10.5% stake, down from 20.7%.
The Reserve Bank of India on Wednesday raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, joining several major central banks in tightening monetary policy to arrest accelerating inflation.
The central bank increased the benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points to a 1-year high of 5.50%, in line with expectations of economists polled by Reuters.
India's economic growth has been strong despite global challenges, Sanjay Malhotra, RBI governor, said in his address on Wednesday, while adding that "inflation and its outlook are not benign, as they were last year."
The monetary policy committee decided to change the policy stance "to calibrated tightening," Malhotra said.
The hike comes as retail inflation in India has been on the rise for 10 straight months , touching 4.8% in August, higher than the RBI's medium-term target of 4%.
Oil rose Wednesday as attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia raised concerns over crude flows from the Middle East even as supplies have been recovering.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery gained 1.17% at $101.76 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November advanced 1.26% at $90.57 per barrel.
Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer of Zaye Capital Markets, said Tuesday that oil remains "caught between improving physical supply and persistent geopolitical risk."
"The sustained ability of the Houthis in Yemen to target oil facilities hundreds of kilometers from the border keeps the risks of a renewed large-scale crude supply disruption present and high, and these risks could worsen if the Houthis feel the need to apply more pressure as a result of losing more territory," said Samer Hasn, senior market analyst at forex trading platform XS.com.
Hong Kong shares fell Wednesday, amid broad declines in other Asian markets as oil prices rose.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index fell 0.65%, with declines led by healthcare and tech sectors, down 1.32% and 0.63%, respectively.
Mainland China market remained closed for the Golden Week holiday.

articles.title_orig: Frankfurt Book Fair 2026: Bertelsmann is the World’s Biggest Book Publisher
articles.title_zh: Frankfurt Book Fair 2026: Bertelsmann is the World’s Biggest Book Publisher
articles.content_orig:
The title of the world’s largest book publisher has changed hands once again, according to data compiled by consultant Rüdiger Wischenbart and the editors from Digital Publishing Report. In the recently released 2025 Global Publishing Ranking, Bertelsmann surpassed the 2024 leader, Thomson Reuters, which slipped to third place. Bertelsmann, the Germany-based owner of Penguin Random House, posted book publishing revenue of $6.98 billion last year, with $5.86 billion coming from PRH. Thomson Reuters’s book revenue rose from $6.24 billion to $6.62 billion, but that wasn’t enough to keep it atop the list.
In second place was RELX, with sales of $6.53 billion. Wolters Kluwer posted a 17% jump in sales to just over $5 billion, moving it into fourth place ahead of Pearson, whose sales increased 7.8% to $4.82 billion.
The scientific publisher Springer Nature (#7) had a solid 2025 with revenue topping $2 billion for the first time thanks to a 18% sales increase over 2024. Japan’s Hitotsubashi Group (#8) stayed in the top 10 thanks in large part to the success of manga publishers Shueisha and Shogakukan.
As noted by Wischenbart, the 10 largest publishers accounted for well over half of all revenue generated by the publishers on the list (56%, up from 55% in 2024). Publishers falling in the 11th to 20th spots accounted for another 20% of revenue.
According to Wischenbart’s analysis, STM and professional publishers accounted for 49% of all revenue of the publishers included in the ranking, while trade publishers generated 32% of sales and educational publishers 19%.
The largest U.S.-based publisher on the list is HarperCollins (#9), which had revenue of $2.15 billion in the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025. McGraw-Hill, another U.S. publisher, was in 10th place, with sales for the fiscal year ended Mar. 31, 2026, holding at $2.10 billion.
The latest ranking does not include Simon & Schuster, because the publisher has not disclosed its revenue since 2023, when it was acquired by the private equity firm KKR. The last reported figure was $1.04 billion, which would put S&S just outside the 20 largest publishers.
Jim Milliot is editor-at-large at Publishers Weekly .

articles.title_orig: U.S. News & World Report Partners with Candid to Bring Agentic AI Survey Innovation to Senior Living
articles.title_zh: U.S. News & World Report Partners with Candid to Bring Agentic AI Survey Innovation to Senior Living
articles.content_orig:
Strategic partnership modernizes how senior living operators capture real-time resident and family feedback.
WASHINGTON , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- U.S. News & World Report, the global authority in healthcare decision support, today announced a strategic partnership with and investment in Candid, an AI-powered engagement start-up serving senior living and post-acute care organizations, to modernize feedback collection and advance resident engagement and quality measurement standards across the senior living industry.
Through the partnership, U.S. News and Candid equip senior living communities to move beyond traditional static questionnaires through AI-powered, conversational engagement tools. The integration expands the tools available to operators to capture real-time insights from residents and their families, turning direct resident and family input into measurable quality improvements.
This collaboration comes at a pivotal time for the senior care sector. With 10,000 Americans reaching retirement age daily – known as "The Peak 65 Phenomenon" – the need for transparent, reliable data to guide family care decisions and evaluate community performance continues to grow. Building on U.S. News' 2026 Best Senior Living ratings , which evaluated communities based on feedback from more than 540,000 consumer surveys, U.S. News continues to lead efforts to standardize resident engagement measures and bring modern, data-driven capabilities to senior living operators and care providers.
"For five years, U.S. News' Best Senior Living ratings have provided families with trusted data and benchmarks as they evaluate their senior living options," said Sumita Singh, executive vice president and general manager of Health at U.S. News. "As millions of older adults enter retirement, improving how senior living communities capture resident and family feedback is a must. Our strategic partnership with Candid reflects our commitment to bringing frictionless technologies to senior living operators so they can gather real-time resident and family feedback across all modalities."
Candid's platform uses interactive voice and text conversations that allow residents, family members and employees to provide feedback in their own words. The platform combines quantitative metrics with qualitative sentiment analysis, identifying recurring themes, emerging operational concerns and trends.
Across current deployments – which span hundreds of senior living communities nationwide – Candid's conversational format averages an approximate 70 percent response rate, drastically outperforming traditional survey channels.
"Senior living organizations have historically had to choose between collecting structured data at scale and having meaningful conversations with residents, families, and employees," said Raphael Rubens, founder and CEO of Candid. "AI allows us to combine both, understand what is driving the feedback and turn those insights into action, ultimately improving the experience and quality of care for residents."
About U.S. News & World Report U.S. News & World Report is the global leader for journalism that empowers consumers, citizens, business leaders and policy officials to make confident decisions in all aspects of their lives and communities. A multifaceted media company, U.S. News provides unbiased rankings, independent reporting and analysis, and consumer advice to millions of people on USNews.com each month. A pillar in Washington for more than 90 years, U.S. News is the trusted home for in-depth and exclusive insights on education, health, politics, the economy, insurance, personal finance, travel, automobiles, real estate, careers and consumer products and services.
About Candid Candid Technology, Inc. ("Candid") is an AI powered engagement platform for senior living and post acute care. Its technology helps organizations collect resident, family, and employee feedback, improve online reputation, understand retention, and automate frontline applicant engagement and interviews. Candid has been deployed across hundreds of communities throughout the United States and is backed by leading investors. For more information, visit callcandid.com .

articles.title_orig: France’s student protests highlight a debt crisis that could spill over to the rest of Europe
articles.title_zh: France’s student protests highlight a debt crisis that could spill over to the rest of Europe
articles.content_orig:
France’s unprecedented wave of student protests has laid bare the country’s growing financial pressures, which will only become more difficult to tackle as Europe’s second-largest economy tries to rein in a ballooning budget deficit.
The country’s finances are in a precarious state. Public debt was more than $4 trillion in June, exceeding the size of the economy, according to the country’s statistics agency . The cost of servicing that debt has climbed by billions of dollars on last year, as bond yields spike .
At the same time, demands on the public purse are rising: Pension costs have climbed because of an aging population while the government looks to spend more on defense.
High school students, meanwhile, have called for a fix to staff shortages, overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school infrastructure.
Solutions to France’s financial troubles have led to social unrest in the past. Efforts to raise the retirement age sparked widespread protests in 2023 .
French school protests grow as workers join students
Last week, the French government proposed deep spending cuts and tax hikes aimed at narrowing the budget deficit, but bond buyers are concerned that fiscal measures may be watered down by lawmakers ahead of presidential elections next year, said Andrew Kenningham, chief European economist at consultancy Capital Economics.
The election could see President Emmanuel Macron ousted by either a far-right or far-left successor, raising questions over the country’s commitment to fiscal discipline. While Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally recently proposed substantial spending cuts meant to stabilize the public finances, her party also remains committed to costly tax reductions, Kenningham said.
“Investors will also be concerned about greater fiscal populism after the elections,” he wrote in a note last week. “There is a big risk that spreads rise a lot further, either before or after next year’s elections.”
Worries about a potential debt crisis in France boiled over last week, leading to a selloff in French bonds and a sharp rise in yields.
The spread between French and German bond yields expanded to its widest level since 2012. That difference in yields means investors are demanding much higher returns to hold debt from France compared with Germany, which is deemed a safer alternative.
The French bond rout has sparked fears of spillovers to other high-yield European debt markets, with some analysts drawing parallels with the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s .
Global bond sell-off deepens, sending borrowing costs higher around the world
Given France’s size and systemic importance, “the potential for contagion into other countries and the Eurozone at large is very large and could potentially cause a serious crisis for the entire region,” Angel Talavera, chief European economist at Oxford Economics, an advisory firm, told CNN.
These worries in large part pushed the euro to its weakest level against the dollar since May 2025 on Monday. The currency, shared by 21 countries in the European Union, is worth around $1.12, having briefly dipped below that level.
The latest ructions in markets could weigh on a fragile economic recovery in Europe, bolstered by investment into artificial intelligence, stronger demand for European exports and higher defense spending in Germany.
Recent survey data showed that activity in manufacturing and services in the euro area increased at its fastest pace in nearly three-and-a-half years last month.
“(Economic) growth is staging a comeback and Europe has shown surprising resilience,” economists at Morgan Stanley wrote in a late September note.
Fall of yet another premier will make it hard for France to fix its finances. What’s behind its debt problem?
High bond yields are a clear risk to that growth, however.
If governments don’t cut spending , “interest rates will continue to go up,” Carsten Brzeski, head of macroeconomics at Dutch bank ING told CNN.
Higher bond yields push up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy, making home and car purchases more expensive and driving down investment. They also make it more expensive for governments to borrow money and force a certain degree of austerity to stop yields from rising further.
Yields on French, German and UK government bonds have broken multi-year records in recent weeks as concerns mount about the sustainability of public debt loads.
Europe’s public finances pose “serious risks to eurozone financial markets and to the economy,” Jack Allen-Reynolds, deputy chief eurozone economist at Capital Economics, told CNN.

articles.title_orig: EU negotiators head to China hoping to curb cheap imports of hybrid electric cars
articles.title_zh: EU negotiators head to China hoping to curb cheap imports of hybrid electric cars
articles.content_orig:
Mood in trade talks said to have changed as EU member states harden demands for protection against Chinese imports
EU trade negotiators are heading to China for two days of crunch talks aimed at sealing a breakthrough deal tackling Beijing’s record £1bn-a-day trade surplus by curbing its exports of cheap hybrid electric cars into Europe .
Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his team fly out on Wednesday and will be negotiating up to the wire in talks scheduled to start the following day and continue late into Friday.
Sources say they hope to achieve “tangible, meaningful and measurable” results before the meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Thursday next week, where China is high on the agenda.
The main focus is on what has been described as a “proof of concept” pilot agreement involving one sector, which is expected to be cars, which could be scaled up for other sectors in the coming months.
Diplomatic efforts to avert a full-scale trade war started at the end of June, albeit with little hope that China could curb exports to the EU given its historic ability to pivot quickly any time trade barriers are put in its path. For example, after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in October 2024 there was a boom in exports of hybrid cars , which were not subject to tariffs.
Last month, the EU asked China to voluntarily restrict hybrid exports to address soaring sales, warning that if they did not restrict them, safeguards – which could include quotas – could be enacted.
It is not known what China’s response was. But sources say the mood in talks has changed as EU member states have hardened demands for protection against Chinese imports that threaten their own industries.
On Monday, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, agreed a “historic U-turn” on its policy on China by siding with the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in authorising effective permission for EU leaders to approve a new instrument to allow them to defend trade by cutting access to the single market at short notice.
In a joint paper with Emmanuel Macron, the two countries spoke of “a massive industrial shock … affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.]”.
The paper called for the use of all existing trade defence tools, but also for a new diversification instrument and “possible additional” new measures to allow the bloc to react when “third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field”.
Andrew Small, a former EU adviser on China, said Šefčovič’s talks will test the resolve of both Beijing and Brussels and will “determine whether China is willing to put sufficiently serious offers on the table”.
Small, who is the Asia director at the European Council on Foreign Relations in Berlin, warned: “China’s most effective tactic may be to draw Europe into a ‘process trap’ offering just enough to delay action, without addressing the forces driving European deindustrialisation.”
after newsletter promotion
Sources say the Franco-German proposals for a new instrument, dubbed a “kill switch”, were born out of frustration, particularly in Paris, that a so-called “trade bazooka” available to Brussels, officially known as the anti-coercion instrument, has never been used.
Paris pushed for the use of the ACI following Trump’s threat of tariffs last year but it never gained traction from others as it could take up to a year to implement.
Handlesblatt, the Germany business newspaper, described Monday’s change in policy as “nothing less than an economic turning point”, with chief political reporter Martin Greive concluding in a hard-hitting column that Merz was “putting an end to years of naiveté towards Beijing”.
“Merz has recognised in recent months that Germany is the epicentre of the China shock 2.0; that there might not be much left of German industry if Germany continues to stand by and watch as China gains enormous export advantages through trillions in subsidies, the unilateral siphoning off of knowhow, and a – to put it mildly – questionable monetary policy,” he wrote.

articles.title_orig: Dow Jones Futures: S&P 500 Hits High As Astera, GE Vernova, Arista Lead Buys, But These Stocks Tumble
articles.title_zh: Dow Jones Futures: S&P 500 Hits High As Astera, GE Vernova, Arista Lead Buys, But These Stocks Tumble
articles.content_orig:
The United States stock market has hit an all-time high as excitement around artificial intelligence continues to fuel a buying frenzy on Wall Street.
The S&P 500, the benchmark stock index, closed 0.58 percent higher on Tuesday, topping the previous peak reached in mid-August.
The Nasdaq Composite, which is more heavily weighted towards tech stocks, also hit a record high, finishing up 0.45 percent.
Tech stocks were among the top performers, with each of the “Magnificent Seven” apart from Meta closing higher.
Amazon led the pack with a 1.95 percent gain, followed by Microsoft and Tesla, which rose 0.78 percent and 0.51 percent, respectively.
Apple and Alphabet both rose 0.22 percent, while Nvidia gained 0.14 percent.
Meta, which has risen more than 20 percent since the launch last month of its new AI assistant, Muse, fell 0.41 percent.
Other big movers in tech included Marvell Technology, which rose 5.81 percent, and Cisco, which gained 4.54 percent.
Keith Lerner, chief investment officer and chief market strategist at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta, Georgia, said the market rally should be seen as a “technology and AI surge”.
“Every bull market has a dominant theme, and technology and AI remain this market’s dominant theme,” Lerner told Al Jazeera.
“Technology and communication services were the only two S&P 500 sectors to rise last month, while the other nine declined.”
Wall Street has shrugged off a host of challenges facing the US economy amid hyperscalers’ multibillion-dollar investments in AI.
Despite the energy crunch caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran and a sell-off of US government bonds partly driven by ballooning government debt, the market is well on track to record its fourth consecutive year of double-digit returns.
The S&P 500 has risen 14 percent so far in 2026, while the Nasdaq Composite is up 18.78 percent.
“Investors remain bullish on the prospects for AI,” Lochlan Halloway, a senior equity strategist at Morningstar Australia, told Al Jazeera.
“They are betting that the money pouring into data centres will earn a good return, and so far that belief has outweighed rising interest rates, more expensive oil and a 10-year bond yield above 5 percent,” Halloway said.
“We are positive on AI too,” Halloway added. “But the range of outcomes is wide, and the market is concentrated in a handful of companies, so the outlook for US shares, and by extension global shares, relies on the AI story continuing to deliver.”
Lerner at Truist Advisory said the market rally had the potential to continue through the end of 2026 given historical trends and expectations for strong corporate earnings.
“We do not expect a straight line higher for markets,” Lerner said.
“Still, the fourth quarter of midterm-election years has produced an average gain of 7 percent and has been positive 84 percent of the time since 1950.”
Lerner said that rising interest rates posed the biggest risk to the upward trend.
“Still, on balance, the weight of the evidence suggests this bull market still has more upside potential,” he said.
Asian stock markets fell on Wednesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong slumping in morning trading.
The Nikkei 225 in Tokyo, Kospi in Seoul and Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong were down 0.79 percent, 1.36 percent and 0.71 percent, respectively, as of 02:30 GMT.
Oil prices, which have been elevated since the start of the war on Iran, rose on Wednesday as traders weighed the fallout of fighting between forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Brent crude futures for December delivery stood at $101.45 a barrel as of 02:30 GMT, up 0.87 percent.

articles.title_orig: Are Chinese foreign agent busts on the rise? Federal officials make another arrest
articles.title_zh: Are Chinese foreign agent busts on the rise? Federal officials make another arrest
articles.content_orig:
by GEOFF HARRIS | The National News Desk
WASHINGTON (TNND)  — A woman accused of acting as an agent of China appeared in federal court in Los Angeles this week after prosecutors said she conducted surveillance last year near Seattle targeting the son of Taiwan’s president.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli said Wanying Zhang was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport.
According to an affidavit, Zhang acted at the direction and control of People’s Republic of China officials to conduct surveillance on family members of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official at their residence in the United States.
The case is the latest in a string of similar arrests pursued by federal officials. Research shows that under the current administration, there have been 60 PRC-related counterintelligence arrests, an 88% increase compared to prior periods.
Among other recent cases, Greg Lui, who was arrested earlier this month for allegedly orchestrating a $300 million illegal AI hardware smuggling ring to China. Plus, Eileen Wang, the former Arcadia, California, mayor, who pleaded guilty this past summer to a federal charge of acting as an unregistered foreign agent for the People’s Republic of China.
After Zhang’s arrest, FBI Director Kash Patel also posted a warning on social media. Writing, “Foreign adversaries take note: America is not your playground.”
When asked whether the number of such cases is likely to rise, Essayli said, “It probably will. And that’s a testament to this administration, the Trump administration and the attorney general, you know, prioritizing the resources of the department.”

articles.title_orig: Yemen’s Houthi Rebels Strike Two Airports in Saudi Arabia
articles.title_zh: Yemen’s Houthi Rebels Strike Two Airports in Saudi Arabia
articles.content_orig:
CAIRO — Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Wednesday claimed attacks on military facilities and airports in neighboring Saudi Arabia as the escalation deepened the latest front in the Iran war and threatened a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz .
The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said on social media that the rebels launched ballistic missiles and drones in the attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, but did not provide evidence.
Flights to and from the airport were briefly disrupted, according to Flightradar24, a tracking platform.
Saree said Abha airport, a frequent target of Houthi drones and missiles, was targeted. The rebels also claimed to have hit an air base in the city of Khamis Mushait and two military bases, Najran and Asir. All are in southwestern Saudi Arabia and near the border with Yemen.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said they intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile north of Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces in recent days have launched a major ground and air offensive against the Houthis in an attempt to retake territory that the rebels seized about a month ago along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait . Those positions gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping as they pursue a blockade of Saudi vessels.
On Monday, officials said forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen recaptured several key areas around the strait.
The fighting has since then centered in and around the crucial town of Dhubab, some 30 miles south of the port city of Mokha, according to both the Houthis and the Yemeni government.
Clashes were also reported in the district of Waziayah in southwestern Taiz province, which links Yemen’s mountainous highlands to the Red Sea, and overlooks roads to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Houthi officials accuse Yemen of deadly market strike
The Houthis also said they launched a missile strike early Wednesday against Yemen’s port city of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government. An Associated Press journalist heard explosions around 2 a.m. (7 p.m. Tuesday ET).
The rebels hit a military camp close to the Aden airport with ballistic missiles, Saree said.
Security authorities in Aden said the Houthis targeted the airport with two missiles, with no casualties. The airport is close to the seat of government.
“The targeting of this vital civilian facility represents a direct threat to the safety of civilians, passengers, employees and flight crews,” the Aden police said in a statement.
The attack on the Aden airport threatened “a humanitarian disaster,” as one missile hit close to the runway just before the scheduled landing of a flight from Cairo, the Human Rights Ministry said.
Flight 603, operated by Yemen’s flagship airline, landed safely in Aden at 3:30 a.m., according to flight tracking platform FlightAware.
The ministry said the missile hit as other passengers were waiting to board their flight to the Saudi coastal city of Jeddah.
“The Houthis believe that they can maximize Saudi economic costs and compel Saudi Arabia to surrender to Houthi demands by striking civilian infrastructure, such as oil facilities and airports,” the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, wrote in an analysis .

articles.title_orig: Georgia governor candidates spar over the economy and Trump in lone debate
articles.title_zh: Georgia governor candidates spar over the economy and Trump in lone debate
articles.content_orig:
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson clashed Tuesday night during their only scheduled debate of this fall’s race for governor in Georgia, taking aim at each other on economic issues, data centers and President Donald Trump.
Public polls show Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta and a former Biden administration official, and Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive, locked in a close race four weeks out from Election Day, with early voting kicking off next week.
The hourlong, town-hall-style debate was largely civil, featuring live and taped questions from voters. Jackson frequently ripped his opponent over her record as mayor, while Bottoms attacked his praise of Trump.
“My opponent has said he wants to be Trump’s favorite governor. He wants to be Trump with a Southern tone. He said there’s not a single policy that he disagrees with Trump on,” Bottoms said in response to a question about the Trump administration’s cuts to federal funding.
“I will stand up to Donald Trump when necessary. I’m not running to be his favorite governor,” she continued.
Jackson responded, “I don’t owe anybody anything,” and said, “Nobody’s ever told me what to do.”
He then invoked Brian Kemp, Georgia’s popular, term-limited governor — the first of multiple times he did so.
“I will stand up to anybody, just like Brian Kemp has done. He works with both parties, both presidents, and he stands up when he disagrees,” Jackson said.
Trump endorsed Jackson’s rival, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, during the Republican gubernatorial primary. But Jackson still attempted to claim the MAGA mantle and leaned heavily into comparing himself to the president. Since winning the nomination in June, he’s backed off that approach and sought to link himself more to Kemp, who had also backed Jones.
Jackson took several shots at Bottoms over her tenure as mayor, accusing her of being responsible for regional inflation in the Atlanta area that he claimed exceeded national inflation rates and pointing to higher crime rates in the city during the Covid-19 pandemic.
“This is the kind of policy that we cannot have in running Georgia, not having people feeling safe to go to work,” Jackson said. “Bad mayors don’t make good governors.”
While the candidates were asked about housing and education, the event focused predominantly on economic issues and affordability, with both candidates repeatedly pressed about how they’d bring down costs. Both focused heavily on tax relief.
Bottoms emphasized her proposals to cut or suspend state or local taxes on a raft of items, like auto insurance, groceries, hygiene products and diapers. Jackson reiterated his promise to cut state income taxes, property taxes and taxes on certain utilities.
Data centers and the controversial surveillance traffic cameras known as Flock cameras also took center stage.
On data centers, Bottoms repeated her desire to implement a pause on new construction. Jackson said he wouldn’t approve new construction as governor without first getting local community approval, establishing environmental standards and getting a commitment that local communities’ power bills would be reduced.
But the two sparred over the issue, as well, with Bottoms accusing Jackson of investing in data centers and Jackson accusing her of having approved building them as mayor.
Bottoms also said she wasn’t opposed to a moratorium on installing new Flock cameras, while Jackson said he was.
The issue of election security — which has hung over Georgia politics for six years — also came up.
Bottoms said she was “deeply concerned about Donald Trump’s rhetoric around our elections.”
Jackson, however, when he was asked whether he thought the U.S. Justice Department should be “overseeing and getting involved” in the state’s elections, deferred to Kemp again.
“I don’t think that’s necessary unless Gov. Kemp thinks it’s necessary,” he said.
Jackson has flooded the airwaves with ads, using tens of millions of dollars of his own money to outspend Bottoms 7-to-1 as of last week .
That disparity has worried many Democrats , who’ve seen this year as a prime opportunity to flip the governorship blue for the first time in 16 years.
Aiding Bottoms is the broader political environment in Georgia and nationally: Trump faces negative approval ratings and voter concerns about his administration’s handling of the economy.
I cover state legislatures, politics and policy — and how those topics coalesce into and intersect with national political trends. Given what state lawmakers have focused on in recent years, my coverage areas tend to veer into reproductive rights, voting rights and education policy. I was born and raised in Milwaukee, and I try to make my native state proud by covering as many of its fascinating political stories as I can.

articles.title_orig: US military will execute Fort Hood shooter by firing squad, a first in 60 years
articles.title_zh: US military will execute Fort Hood shooter by firing squad, a first in 60 years
articles.content_orig:
An undated handout image of Hasan that was released by authorities in 2012
The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Nidal Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that US defence secretary Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.
The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote on X.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
Watch: Why is America running out of execution drugs? , external
Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.
Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.
The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.
Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.
Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.
How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.
Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.
The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

articles.title_orig: Calm Down, China and America Are Not Destined for War
articles.title_zh: Calm Down, China and America Are Not Destined for War
articles.content_orig:
For much of the past decade, debate about China and the United States has been shadowed by a familiar warning: when a rising power challenges an established one, war becomes more likely. The “Thucydides Trap,” popularized by the political scientist Graham Allison, has supplied a compelling framework for interpreting their rivalry. In public discussion, however, a warning about the dangers of power transitions too often hardens into a prediction that conflict is unavoidable.
That distinction matters. Allison himself does not regard war as inevitable. Yet the fatalistic version of his argument has become so pervasive that almost every trade dispute, technological restriction, or diplomatic confrontation can be presented as another step toward a collision. Such a reading leaves too little room for political judgment, negotiated compromises, or the possibility that leaders can recognize the costs of escalation and act accordingly.
My assessment, informed by exchanges with strategic scholars, business leaders, and participants in unofficial Chinese-American dialogues, is more guardedly hopeful. Despite their differences, leaders in Beijing and Washington retain powerful reasons to manage competition. Their diplomatic contacts suggest that both governments understand the dangers of allowing individual disputes to determine the entire relationship. Neither has to abandon its interests to recognize that an uncontrolled confrontation would threaten them.
China’s growing ability to shape that relationship is also changing its dynamics. Meanwhile, two features of American politics deserve closer attention: domestic division complicates the construction of a durable China strategy, and some economic disputes with Beijing resemble the quarrels Washington routinely has with its allies. Neither observation eliminates the risks of rivalry. Both challenge the assumption that every disagreement signals an approaching war.
The balance of power provides a useful starting point. Measured at market exchange rates, the American economy remains substantially larger than China’s. Purchasing power parity, which adjusts for differences in domestic prices, produces a different ranking, placing China first. These measures capture different aspects of economic strength. Neither, taken alone, can tell us how effectively a country will translate its resources into technological leadership, military capability, or diplomatic influence.
China’s industrial scale is harder to dispute. Its manufacturing value added reached approximately 34.7 trillion yuan in 2025, and, according to China’s National Bureau of Statistics, it has ranked first globally for 16 consecutive years. The breadth of that industrial base gives Beijing capabilities that the United States would struggle to reproduce quickly. Research and development spending reached roughly 3.9 trillion yuan in 2025, reflecting the resources China is committing to technological advancement.
The country has built substantial capacity in solar manufacturing, electric vehicles, and robotics, alongside a growing presence in artificial intelligence research and patenting. These strengths do not establish superiority in every technology. They do, however, make it increasingly difficult to imagine a strategy that permanently excludes China from the industries likely to shape future economic growth. Industrial capacity is a source of bargaining power as well as national income.
The United States retains formidable advantages of its own. The dollar’s international role, deep financial markets, leading research institutions, extensive alliances, and capacity to project military power all give Washington considerable influence. Those assets will not disappear simply because China continues to grow. The relationship is therefore better understood as an uneven distribution of strengths than as a straightforward reversal in which one country replaces the other across every measure of power.
In my view, this balance creates an opening for strategic stabilization. Washington has limited ability to halt China’s development, while Beijing has strong reasons to avoid a confrontation that would endanger its own economic gains. China’s ambitions need not require the dismantling of every American advantage. Both governments can defend their interests while accepting that an effort to impose comprehensive defeat on the other would carry enormous costs.
American domestic politics complicates this calculation. Analysts sometimes treat congressional hawkishness, campaign rhetoric, and executive policy as expressions of a single, coherent strategy. In practice, partisan polarization, disputes between Congress and the presidency, and tensions between federal and state priorities can pull policy in different directions. Elections can change the instruments of foreign policy even when the underlying concern about China persists.
That distinction is essential. There is considerable continuity in American suspicion of Beijing, but agreement about a rival does not automatically produce agreement about how to compete with it. Tariffs, industrial subsidies, export controls, alliance commitments, and diplomatic engagement impose different costs on different constituencies. A strategy that appears unified at the level of political rhetoric can become far less coherent when officials must allocate resources or sustain it across administrations.
Domestic pressures further constrain Washington’s choices. Social division, the erosion of manufacturing in some communities, and inequality absorb political attention and public resources. Taking a hard line on China can be an effective campaign message without resolving any of those problems. Analysts who assume that rhetoric translates smoothly into a sustained grand strategy risk overstating the consistency of American power and understating the difficulty of mobilizing it.
The nature of bilateral friction also deserves a more discriminating assessment. Disputes over trade, technology, and diplomacy are likely to remain ordinary features of Chinese-American relations. But economic disagreement does not, by itself, distinguish this relationship from all others. The United States regularly clashes with partners whose security and prosperity are closely bound to its own, sometimes with strikingly hostile public language.
Washington and European governments have argued over digital taxes, subsidies, steel tariffs, and market access. Canada and the United States have repeatedly disputed softwood lumber and border policy. Japan has faced American pressure over agricultural access and the costs of hosting U.S. forces. These quarrels can inflict serious economic damage while remaining within a broader relationship that both sides wish to preserve.
There are obvious limits to the comparison. Disagreements between allies do not carry the same strategic implications as disputes between nuclear-armed competitors. Nevertheless, their existence should caution against treating every commercial confrontation with China as evidence that war is drawing closer. The question is how governments manage conflicting interests and whether they have credible mechanisms for preventing a dispute in one area from overwhelming cooperation in another.
In the dialogues I have attended, I have encountered substantial support for that approach. Scholars and business leaders recognize that the noise of domestic politics does not erase the need for crisis management. Diplomatic, economic, and military communication matters precisely because competition is intensifying. Such channels cannot guarantee restraint, but their maintenance gives governments a means of clarifying intentions before a misunderstanding becomes a confrontation.
Meetings between national leaders can serve a similar purpose. Beyond their ceremonial functions, they allow governments to test assumptions, communicate limits, and establish expectations. Nuclear deterrence supplies an especially

articles.title_orig: Chinese woman snaps up nearly 200 parking spots to flip to neighbours for profit
articles.title_zh: Chinese woman snaps up nearly 200 parking spots to flip to neighbours for profit
articles.content_orig:
Residents argue that parking is a vital community asset that should not be monopolised by anyone seeking financial gain from resale
A woman in central China invested 14 million yuan (US$2 million) to acquire 196 parking spaces in a residential community, later selling them at a significant mark-up, which led to furious residents suing her.
The lawsuit centred around a residential block, the name of which was not disclosed, located in Changsha, Hunan province.
The property project was completed and put on the market in 2018. At the time, many were sceptical about the community’s prospects due to a lack of essential public facilities such as shops, schools, and public transport options. Consequently, there was little interest in both the flats and the parking spaces, according to Hunan TV.
Despite this pessimism, a woman surnamed Wu snapped up 196 parking spots in a single transaction, representing 40 per cent of the project’s total parking inventory, for a sum of 14 million yuan. The developer, facing severe cash constraints, agreed to her purchase.

Oops, something went wrong
The company is reportedly looking for about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt.
On SpaceX's August earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said the company had "decided to build exclusively on Nvidia" for its AI initiatives.
CFO Bret Johnsen previously hinted at full-year capital spending near $65 billion for SpaceX.
SpaceX shares fell 1% in after-hours trading on Tuesday after reports that the company is seeking $40 billion in financing to buy Nvidia chips, a fresh sign of how much capital the AI buildout is consuming.
The rocket manufacturing company's financing effort is expected to be led by Apollo Global Management, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The company is looking for about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt.

Pimco was among a small group of lenders in talks to fund the deal, the report said, adding that the transaction is expected to close in 2027. SpaceX and Nvidia did not confirm the report, the newspaper said.
The borrowing would tighten a tie Musk has already made public. On SpaceX's August earnings call, he said the company had "decided to build exclusively on Nvidia" for its AI initiatives because he considered the Vera Rubin platform the best AI architecture, and that SpaceX valued the partnership.
For Nvidia, a committed buyer of that size helps amid rising competition from rival chipmakers.
SpaceX's AI effort is now the bulk of the company, not a side project. After folding xAI into the group in February, it has been building the Colossus data-center clusters and renting that capacity to outside customers while also training its own Grok models.
The company's capital expenditures were $18.4 billion in the second quarter, and $15.8 billion of that went to AI infrastructure, about 86% of the total, against roughly $1.4 billion for Starlink and $1.2 billion for the space business. First-half spending was about $28.5 billion, while operations generated only about $3.5 billion of cash.
CFO Bret Johnsen told analysts on the August 4 earnings call that the next two quarters should look "very similar," which would put full-year capital spending near $65 billion if that pace holds. He said new compute capital is paying back in less than a year, and the company is aiming for a $100 billion annualized revenue run rate by year-end.

articles.title_orig: Fuel industry warns truck stops not to sell red dye diesel after Trump lifts restrictions
articles.title_zh: Fuel industry warns truck stops not to sell red dye diesel after Trump lifts restrictions
articles.content_orig:
Truck stops nationwide were warned to “proceed with caution” Tuesday by a major industry group after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to promote the use of “red dye” diesel fuel.
Red dye diesel is exempt from federal excise taxes because it is intended for farm equipment and other off-road uses.
The order, signed before farmers in Nebraska on Monday night, aims to bring down fuel prices by “temporarily” allowing highway use of red dye diesel fuel, according to a White House statement .
U.S. voters are deeply frustrated by the high price of gas, and the Trump administration is under intense pressure to bring down fuel costs before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Monday’s order instructs Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to “defer certain diesel fuel tax payment obligations and to provide penalty relief to the extent permitted by law.”
It does not waive the federal taxes, because only Congress can eliminate a tax.
Following Trump’s directive, the Energy Marketers of America warned gas stations to “proceed with caution.”
“Whether relief is available, whom it covers, and on what conditions depend on Treasury determinations and guidance not yet issued,” the group said. “Deferral is not forgiveness.”
Moreover, the order does not “resolve EPA or state restrictions” on the dyed variety of diesel fuel, the EMA said.
Other trucking and gas industry groups sounded a similar note of caution.
“The White House appears to be trying to encourage the supply chain to move toward selling dyed fuel in non-traditional ways,” the Society of Independent Gasoline Marketers of America and the National Association of Truck Stop Owners said in a note to their members.
“We do not expect most reputable diesel retailers and fuel marketers to do this,” they said. “First, the tax is still owed, so there’s limited upside.”
In addition, “the logistical challenges outweigh any visible upside: Residual dye lingers in tanks and fuel systems.”
For most fuel sellers, “the liability and customer risk outweigh any temporary, uncertain benefit.”
The White House did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
A group representing independent long-haul truckers also suggested Trump’s move would provide little benefit to its members.
“Allowing the wider use of red-dyed diesel will provide minimal relief. Market stability is essential to bring down costs for the long haul,” said Todd Spencer, president of the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association.
Since the war with Iran began, the price of diesel has surged from $3.76 per gallon to $6.32 as of Tuesday, a nearly 70% increase.
The Iran conflict is not the only conflict contributing to diesel’s skyrocketing price.
A recent escalation of the Ukraine-Russia war has included strikes by Ukrainian drones on Russian refineries.
Russia, traditionally one of the world’s large diesel exporters, has responded to the attacks by imposing a diesel export ban through at least the end of October.
Trump has urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russia’s diesel infrastructure .
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters in early September . “There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”
Oil prices also remain sharply elevated since the beginning of the year. Brent crude oil, which traded Tuesday night above $101 per barrel, is up more than 66% since the start of the year.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Drone Attack Sets Fire On Oil Tanker With 23 Indian Crew Members
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Drone Attack Sets Fire On Oil Tanker With 23 Indian Crew Members
articles.content_orig:
Two injured crew members from one of the ships have been sent for treatment
A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say.
A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued.
Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable".
Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said.
The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania.
It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board.
A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched.
Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain.
Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan.
Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law".
He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable."
He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning.
"Commercial ships â and innocent crews â are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning."
"Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable."
Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea.
A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media.
On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
